WhatsApp — job photos and real-time updatesAll completion photos, arrival messages, and departure messages go via WhatsApp. Real-time delivery, automatic timestamps, permanent record. This is our evidence system.
Message Bonnie on arrival — Arrived at [address] [time]Your official start time record.
Message Bonnie on departure — Completed [address] leaving now [time]Your official finish time record.
Text or call — urgent job communicationIssues, problems, questions mid-job that cannot wait.
Email — formal and document mattersInvoices, employment documents, contracts, anything requiring a signature.
Never communicate directly with clients about job changes or problemsTell them Bonnie will be in touch — then contact Bonnie immediately.

Working as a team on site

Bond cleans and sellers cleans always have a minimum of 2 staff on site. Airbnb turnovers may be solo or teams depending on property size — Bonnie confirms this at booking.

When working as a team:
Split tasks intelligently from the start
One person pre-soaks the oven while the other starts vacuuming. Communicate what you are doing and when it is done.
Never assume someone else checked something
If a room is your responsibility — you check it. Confirm verbally, do not assume.
Communicate openly if you are running behind
Better to flag it early than have the job run over without warning to Bonnie.
The door-shut system is a team tool
When you close a door, your team knows that room is done. It keeps the standard honest and prevents double-handling.

The re-clean guarantee

WoodBClean provides a re-clean guarantee on all bond cleans. If a real estate agent identifies a genuine issue, we return at no extra cost to the client.

This means: get it right the first time, every time. Your photos are your evidence that you did. If an agent claims something was not cleaned and your photos show it was — the photos win the argument.

If there is ever a complaint — do not contact the client or agent directly. Call Bonnie immediately and send your photos.

The quality self-inspection — before leaving any job

Before leaving, walk every room with fresh eyes. Ask: would I be happy coming home to this? If the answer is no for any area — fix it before you leave.
Glass, windows, and mirrors — streak-free from every angle
Check from multiple angles in different light. Streaks are easiest to see when light hits at an angle.
Tops of doors and ceiling fans
The most commonly missed areas — and the first places an eagle-eyed agent checks.
Skirting boards — all the way around every room
Get down to skirting board level. Dust accumulates here and it is a standard inspection point.
No product residue anywhere
White residue from products left on surfaces means poor rinsing. Check every surface you have cleaned.
Bins emptied and relined
Every bin in the property — kitchen, bathrooms, bedrooms.
Floors dry, clean, no footprints
Floors are the last thing you clean — do not walk back on them.

Attention to detail — seeing what others miss

The difference between a good clean and an excellent one is noticing what most people walk past. Your eye should be constantly scanning — not just for what you were asked to clean, but for what clearly needs cleaning.
1
If you're there and it's dirty — clean it
You were asked to wipe a door frame. You notice sticky residue and built-up grime that comes off with a fingernail. That is your signal — stop, get the right product, and finish the job properly. You don't need to be asked. It's what the client is paying for.
2
Look across surfaces at a low angle
Fingerprints, smears, and dust are invisible front-on. Look across benchtops, glass and surfaces at an angle with a light source behind you. You will see things you'd otherwise walk straight past.
3
Check edges, corners, tracks and hinges
Grime accumulates exactly where it is hardest to reach — window tracks, door edges, inside architrave corners, under the lip of rangehoods, inside cupboard hinges. These are the details that tell a client you actually cleaned the property, not just wiped the obvious surfaces.
4
Ask: would Bonnie be happy with this?
Before you move on from any area, ask honestly whether it meets the standard you'd want as the client coming home. If something feels unfinished — it probably is. Go back.

Scenario: You're cleaning a kitchen benchtop as requested. You notice the rangehood filter is visibly greasy and the splashback has dried food splatters. Nobody specifically asked you to clean these. What do you do — and why?

Clean them. You are on the job, you can see they need attention, and you have the products and the time. A client paying for a kitchen clean expects the kitchen to be clean — not just the specific surfaces that were listed. If it would require significantly more time than agreed, message Bonnie first. But for things you can see while you're standing there — just do it. This is what separates average cleaners from excellent ones.

The 11 things agents and clients actually fail people on

These are not the obvious things. Everyone cleans the toilet and the sink. These are the spots that separate a good clean from a perfect one — and they are exactly what agents and property managers look for first.
1
Window tracks
The single most common fail point. Dirt, dust, and dead insects pack into these channels. Spray, let dwell, use a small brush or old toothbrush, wipe clean. Agents check these every single time.
2
Dishwasher filter
Pull it out, rinse it under hot water, scrub with a brush. Most tenants never do this. Agents and clients open the dishwasher and this is the first thing they check.
3
Rangehood filter
Remove, soak in hot soapy water or degreaser, scrub with a brush, rinse and replace. Grease builds up here invisibly. A clogged rangehood filter is a guaranteed fail.
4
Inside cupboards and drawers
Every shelf, every drawer, wiped out completely. Crumbs, grime, forgotten debris. Agents open every single cupboard. If it is not clean inside, the whole clean fails.
5
Tops of ceiling fans — both sides
The underside is obvious. The top of each blade collects a thick layer of dust that falls when the fan is turned on. Use a damp microfibre cloth over the top of each blade. Do not use a dry cloth — it just moves the dust into the air.
6
Light switches and power points
Every light switch plate, every power point surround — wiped clean with a damp cloth. These accumulate fingerprints, grease, and grime that is very visible at eye level. Never spray directly — spray onto cloth first.
7
Door frame tops
Stand on a step if needed and wipe the top of every door frame. Dust settles here undisturbed for months. If an agent runs their finger across a door frame top and it comes away grey — the clean fails.
8
Exhaust fans
Every bathroom exhaust fan grille — vacuumed first, then wiped with a damp cloth. Dust and lint pack into these grilles. They are directly in the sightline when you look up in a bathroom.
9
Stove drip trays and burner grates
Remove drip trays and burner grates, soak in hot degreaser solution, scrub thoroughly, dry before replacing. Baked-on food residue on these surfaces is a common fail. Do not leave them soaking and forget to replace them.
10
Grout lines
Grout between tiles — especially in bathrooms and kitchens — collects mould and grime. Use a grout cleaner or bathroom product with dwell time. An old toothbrush is the best tool for stubborn grout lines. Agents compare grout to the original condition.
11
Wall marks — especially near light switches and door handles
Scuff marks, fingerprints, and smudges on painted walls. Use a damp cloth with a small amount of all-purpose cleaner. Test in a hidden area first — some paints are not washable. Document any marks that were there before you started.
Professional tip: When you finish a job — walk through the property as if you are the agent doing the inspection. Look at the window tracks. Open a cupboard. Run your finger along a door frame top. If it passes your own inspection, it will pass theirs.

The first 5 minutes determine the next 5 hours

Before you pick up a single cloth, before you plug in the vacuum, before you do anything — read the environment. Walk the property. Look at what you are actually dealing with. This is what Bonnie means when she says WoodBClean cleaners understand what they are doing.

A cleaner who walks in and immediately starts cleaning is guessing. A WoodBClean professional reads the job first, then executes it with a plan.

What to look for on your walk-through

1
Size and condition — how long will this actually take?
Is it a light clean or a heavy clean? A property that hasn't been touched in months needs a different approach and different time allocation than one that was cleaned 2 weeks ago. Assess honestly, and if the job looks significantly larger than briefed — message Bonnie before you start.
2
Pre-existing damage — photograph before you touch anything
Every scratch, chip, stain, broken item, mark on a wall. This is not optional and it is not about distrust — it is about protecting yourself and the client. Send photos to Bonnie immediately on arrival. This is your legal protection.
3
Problem areas — where does this job need extra attention?
Is the oven particularly bad? Heavy mould in the shower? Ground-in grout? These areas need product applied early — dwell time does the work. Identify them on your walk-through, apply product immediately, and let it work while you do other tasks.
4
Surface types — what am I working with?
Timber floors? Natural stone benchtops? Gold tapware? Delicate paintwork? Your walk-through tells you which products are safe to use where. A professional doesn't discover marble benchtops after they've already sprayed acid on them.
5
Anything unusual — and does Bonnie need to know?
Evidence of pests, water damage, safety hazards, or anything that significantly changes the scope of the job. Message Bonnie before proceeding. Use your common sense — if something seems wrong, it probably is.

The 7-day return policy — and why the goal is to never use it

WoodBClean offers a 7-day return policy. If a client identifies something genuinely missed within 7 days — we come back and fix it at no charge.

This policy exists because we stand behind our work. But the goal — Bonnie's personal standard for every job — is to never need to use it.

A completed clean means: you have walked the property at the end with the same critical eye you'd use if you were the client coming home. You've asked yourself "would I be happy with this?" in every room. And you leave knowing the answer is yes.
The WoodBClean standard isn't "good enough to avoid a callback." It's "I'd be proud to put my name on this." That's the difference.

Room sequence — there's no single right answer, but there are wrong ones

Bonnie's approach: always vacuum and dust first. After that, the sequence depends on the size and condition of the property. A small apartment clean might go kitchen → bathroom → bedroom → floors. A heavy bond clean in a 4-bedroom house is a different job entirely.

What matters is the logic behind your sequence — not memorising a fixed order.

The logic that drives every sequence

Vacuum and dust always come first — before any wet cleaning. Wet debris on an unvacuumed floor turns into a paste that smears. Dust falls downward onto surfaces you've already wiped. Vacuum and dust, then wet clean.
Apply product to problem areas immediately on arrival — oven, grout, shower screen. Dwell time is free work. Apply at the start, clean it later. Never wait until you get to that area before applying product.
Work room by room, top to bottom — ceiling fans first, floors last. Close the door when done. Never half-finish a room and move to the next.
Floors are always last — the final act of every room. You cannot walk on a mopped floor to clean something else. Floors go last.
Exit the property clean — as you leave each room, close the door. Walk out through the property in reverse order so your exit path is the least-cleaned area, not the most.

A typical sequence for a standard residential clean

This is a guide, not a rule. Adjust for the specific property.
1
Walk-through — photograph, assess, apply product to problem areas
Pre-existing damage photos sent to Bonnie. Oven and shower product applied immediately to dwell.
2
Vacuum entire property — all rooms, top to bottom
Ceiling fans, vents, walls, skirting boards, floors. Entire property vacuumed before any wet cleaning begins.
3
Bathrooms — walls, vanity, toilet, shower, floor
Most contaminated area, most product use. Done while product from step 1 has been dwelling. Close door when complete.
4
Kitchen — oven (product has been dwelling), rangehood, benches, sink, cupboards, appliances
The oven was soaking since arrival. Scrub and wipe now. Everything else top to bottom. Close door when complete.
5
Bedrooms and living areas — dust, surfaces, windows, sills
Lightest contamination. Work quickly and systematically. Close doors when complete.
6
All floors — mop in sequence, room by room, working toward exit
Fresh water per room. Figure-8 technique. Work backwards toward the front door.
7
Final walk-through — agent's eye view
Walk every room. Look at what the client or agent will see. Fix anything that doesn't pass your own inspection.
8
Photos — all rooms, key areas, sent to Bonnie before leaving
WhatsApp photos from inside the property. Timestamp is your completion record.

Dwell time — the most misunderstood concept in cleaning

Dwell time is how long a cleaning product needs to stay wet on a surface to actually do its job. Most cleaners — including experienced ones — spray a product and wipe it off almost immediately. This achieves almost nothing.

The active ingredients in a cleaning product need contact time with the surface to break down grease, kill bacteria, or dissolve soap scum. If you wipe before that time is up, you are just moving product around. The surface is not clean — it looks clean.

Dwell time guide — Clean Like A Pro range

Product Minimum dwell Heavy build-up Key rule
PRO Shower3–5 min10–15 minApply on arrival — clean at end of room sequence
PRO Degreaser (oven)10–15 min20–30 minApply the moment you arrive — always
PRO Bathroom & Toilet2–3 min5 minUnder toilet rim — let it work before scrubbing
PRO Mould5–10 min15+ minMore dwell = more effective than more scrubbing
PRO Harmony / Multi-Purpose30 sec – 1 min2–3 minGeneral surfaces — spray and work in sections

How to use dwell time efficiently — it's not wasted time

The mistake cleaners make is thinking dwell time slows them down. Done right, it makes you faster.
1
Apply product to all problem areas as soon as you arrive
Oven gets degreaser. Shower gets PRO Shower. Any mould gets PRO Mould. Do this before you do anything else — your walk-through identifies these areas.
2
Go do other work while the product dwells
Vacuum the rest of the property. Clean the bedroom. The product is working for you while you work elsewhere — for free.
3
Return when dwell time is complete — agitate and wipe
The product has done the hard work. You scrub or wipe, and the grime comes off with far less effort than if you had wiped immediately.
💡
The oven rule: Apply PRO Degreaser the moment you walk into any property. Every single time. Even if you think the oven isn't bad — apply it anyway. It costs 30 seconds on arrival and saves you 20 minutes of scrubbing later.

Core principles only matter if you can apply them under pressure. These questions check whether you'd make the right call on a real job.

What is a bond clean?

A bond clean is an end-of-lease clean required to meet real estate inspection standards so the tenant receives their bond back. At WoodBClean our bond cleans cover every surface, every room, inside and out — decks and patios included. Always a minimum of 2 staff on site. Backed by our re-clean guarantee.

What is a sellers clean?

A sellers clean prepares a property for sale — making it look its absolute best for real estate photography and open homes. Same depth as a bond clean but the finish standard is elevated — every surface polished and photo-ready. Real estate photos are often taken immediately after your work.

Key differences from a bond clean

Every reflective surface polished streak-freeGlass, mirrors, taps, tiles, stainless steel. Check from multiple angles in good light.
Final polish pass is mandatory in every roomAfter the full clean, a complete second pass on all reflective surfaces before closing the door.
Windows inside AND out — alwaysExternal windows are always included. Real estate photos will show streaks on the outside.
Pressure washing — only if confirmed by Bonnie before the jobDriveways, paths, decks, exterior walls.
Carpet cleaning via subcontractor — if required, booked separately by Bonnie
Acid washing for heavy mineral deposits requires explicit Bonnie approval and full PPE. Never proceed without authorisation.

Sellers clean checklist

How agents actually inspect — and how to think like one

Understanding what a property manager is looking for — and why — changes how you approach every bond clean. They are not looking for a good clean. They are looking for reasons to deduct from the bond. Once you understand that, you clean differently.
1
They start with the entry condition report
The entry condition report documents the property's condition when the tenant moved in. The agent compares the property against this report. Your job is to get the property back to that condition — or better. Anything below that standard is a potential deduction.
2
They inspect in a specific order
Kitchen first — always. It is the hardest to clean and the easiest to fail. Then bathrooms, then living areas, then bedrooms, then outside. If the kitchen fails, the whole inspection fails. Start there, spend the most time there.
3
They open everything
Every cupboard, every drawer, every appliance. Oven, dishwasher, washing machine, fridge (if included). Every single one. Clean inside every door, every shelf, every drawer lining.
4
They look at eye level and above
Light switches, power points, door handles — at eye level. Door frame tops, rangehood, ceiling fans, exhaust fans — above eye level. Most amateur cleans only cover below eye level. Professional cleans cover everything.
5
They compare — not just check
If the entry condition report shows a clean grout line and the exit condition shows stained grout — that is a deduction. If the report shows no marks on the wall and the exit shows scuffs — that is a deduction. Your clean needs to match or exceed the original condition.
Photo evidence protects you. Before you start a bond clean — photograph any pre-existing damage, stains, or marks. Date-stamp the photos. If a dispute arises, you have proof of what was already there when you arrived.
The best bond cleaners think like agents. When you finish, walk through the property as an agent would — entry condition report in hand — and look for anything that would justify a deduction. If you find it, fix it before they do.

The finer details — where bond callbacks actually come from

Bonnie's experience is clear: callbacks don't come from missed kitchens or dirty bathrooms. They come from the small things — the details that take an extra 30 seconds each and that most cleaners skip because they assume no one will look. Agents look. Every time.

The finer details checklist — go through every one

!
Window tracks and sliding door tracks
The single most common callback item. Agents run their finger along every track. Dirt, dead insects, and debris collect in the corners. Use the PRO Utility tool with a small brush attachment. Each corner individually — don't just run the vacuum along the centre.
!
Corners — floors, ceilings, and walls
Corners collect dust and cobwebs that are invisible from the middle of the room. Check every corner in every room: floor corners, ceiling corners, where the wall meets the skirting board. Get down and look. Agents do.
!
Behind and under appliances — fridge gap, washing machine
The gap beside and behind the fridge. Under the washing machine. These areas are almost never cleaned between tenancies and they accumulate remarkable amounts of debris. If you can move the appliance safely — do it.
!
Fly screens
Almost always missed. Remove each fly screen, wash with warm water and a soft brush, rinse, dry before replacing. An agent will remove a fly screen and check the frame.
!
Tops of doors and door frames
Run your flat microfibre cloth along every door frame top. If it comes away with dust — the agent will find it. Do every door in the property.
!
Inside of cupboard hinges and drawer runners
Grease, crumbs, and debris collect in hinge recesses and inside drawer runners. A damp cloth in the hinge recess, a wipe along every drawer runner.
!
Exhaust fans — bathroom and kitchen
The grill cover collects lint and grease over years. Remove the cover, wipe with PRO Degreaser in the kitchen, PRO Bathroom in the bathroom. Let dry before replacing.
!
Under the toilet rim
Apply PRO Bathroom and Toilet under the rim on arrival — let it dwell. Scrub with the toilet brush on the way back through. Agents lift the seat. They look under the rim. They always do.
!
Grout lines — especially in corners and at floor level
Agents use torches on grout. Mould, soap scum, and discolouration in grout lines are a very common deduction reason. PRO Shower on dwell, stiff brush in the grout lines, rinse thoroughly.
!
Light switch and power point surrounds
Finger marks, scuffs, and grime build up around light switches over years. Clean the switch plate and the wall immediately around it. Every switch, every room.
The 30-second rule: Every item on this list takes under 30 seconds to do correctly. The cost of skipping them is a callback, a re-clean, and a client who questions whether WoodBClean is worth the price. Do them all, every time.

Callbacks — the 7-day return policy and how it works

WoodBClean offers a 7-day return policy on bond cleans. If something genuine was missed and the agent or owner identifies it within 7 days — we come back and fix it. This is a commitment to quality, not an expectation of failure.

Callbacks happen in every cleaning business. How you handle them is what separates a professional operation from everyone else.

The callback process — step by step

1
Agent or owner contacts Bonnie directly
All callback communication goes through Bonnie — not through you. If a client or agent contacts you directly about a missed item, acknowledge politely and tell them Bonnie will be in touch today. Do not negotiate, do not make promises, do not visit the property without Bonnie's instruction.
2
Photos of the missed area must be provided
Bonnie requires photographic evidence of the specific area before any callback is actioned. This protects WoodBClean — it confirms whether the area was missed by the cleaner or damaged/dirtied after the clean. Your completion photos from the job are Bonnie's comparison point.
3
Bonnie does internal checks
Bonnie reviews your WhatsApp completion photos, assesses the callback claim, and communicates with the agent. This is why your completion photos must be comprehensive — they are your professional record and your protection.
4
If the callback is confirmed — return within 24–48 hours
If Bonnie confirms the item was missed — a return is organised promptly. Focus only on the specific area identified. Do not re-clean the entire property. Before and after photos of the callback area are sent to Bonnie immediately on completion.
5
Learn from it — every callback is a training moment
If you receive a callback, Bonnie will discuss it with you. It is not a personal attack. It is information that makes you a better cleaner. The goal is that each cleaner's callback rate trends toward zero over time.

Why your completion photos are critical

Bonnie cannot defend a callback without evidence of what was cleaned. Your WhatsApp completion photos — sent before you leave the property — are that evidence.

For every bond clean, before you leave, photograph:
Oven interior — door open, racks in, door glass visible
Shower screen and grout — close up, showing clarity
Stovetop and rangehood
Bathroom vanity and toilet
Window tracks — at least two examples
Each room overview shot (door open, full room visible)
💡
The cleaners at WoodBClean with the lowest callback rates are the ones who take the most completion photos. The photos aren't just protection — they're a habit that forces a final check of every area before you put the camera away.

Sellers cleans — cleaning for the camera

Bonnie's instruction for every sellers clean, in her own words:
"Slow down. Polish everything. This is about perfection — because a camera will pick up if you've left wipe marks, smudges, or water droplets."
Real estate photography happens immediately after your work. The photos go on Domain, realestate.com.au, and every marketing material for the property. A smudge on a mirror or a watermark on a tap will be in every photo, seen by thousands of potential buyers.

A sellers clean is not a bond clean done quickly. It is a bond clean done slowly, with a second polishing pass on every reflective surface.

The photography standard — what this means in practice

1
Every reflective surface gets two passes
Clean it. Then polish it. Mirrors, glass, taps, tiles, stainless steel appliances, rangehood — everything that reflects light gets cleaned and then polished dry with a clean dry microfibre. Check from multiple angles in natural light. What you can see, a camera can see.
2
No wipe marks — direction matters
Always wipe glass and mirrors in a single direction — not circular. Circular motions leave visible arc marks. Horizontal or vertical strokes, then a dry buff. Hold a torch or use natural light at a 45-degree angle to check for streaks before moving on.
3
Water droplets are not cosmetic — they're a failure
A tap with water droplets on it tells the buyer the bathroom was cleaned carelessly. Every tap, every shower head, every bath spout — dry polished to a shine. Use a dry microfibre, buff in circular motions last, then a straight wipe to remove any circular marks.
4
Windows inside AND out — and check from outside
External window streaks are caught immediately in photography. Clean inside, then outside. Then step back and look at the window from outside in natural light before moving on. If you can see streaks — the camera will see streaks.
5
The final walk-through is different for a sellers clean
Don't just check cleanliness — check presentation. Are the blinds even? Is the shower screen perfectly squeegeed? Are there any smudges from where you touched a surface after polishing it? A sellers clean final check is slower and more thorough than any other job type.

Sellers clean photo gate — before you leave

Send Bonnie these photos from inside the property before leaving. These go to the agent as proof of completion.
Kitchen — benchtops, sink, stovetop, oven, rangehood all in one photo
Bathroom — mirror, shower screen, taps, vanity bench polished
Windows — at least 2 examples showing streak-free glass
Each main room — overview shot showing floors and surfaces
Any feature area that the property is being marketed on (views, deck, pool area)

Airbnb and short-stay cleans

Airbnb and short-stay cleans have strict presentation and hygiene standards — each with specific protocols, safety requirements, and approaches that differ significantly from standard residential cleans.

Module 7 recap3 quick questions before Module 8
Module 7 recap — 3 questions

Two Airbnb clean types — know the difference

ST
Standard turnover — your default for every Airbnb job
Every Airbnb job is a standard turnover unless Bonnie explicitly specifies otherwise in the job brief. Full clean, linen change, restock, beds made to presentation standard.
DC
Deep clean — only when Bonnie specifies in writing
Bond clean level throughout. Bonnie will always confirm this before you arrive. If it is not mentioned in the brief — it is a standard turnover. Never self-upgrade without Bonnie confirmation.

PPE for Airbnb cleans

Gloves — all bathroom work, no exceptionsBathrooms contain biological contamination. Gloves on for the entire time you are in any bathroom regardless of what you are doing.
Gloves — all chemical product use throughout the propertyAny time you are applying any product — gloves on.
Gloves optional for dry tasksMaking beds with fresh linen, restocking sealed supplies, emptying bin liners — use your judgement.
Deep clean — full PPE throughout as per bond clean
Time pressure is real on standard turnovers. Typically 2–4 hours between guest checkout and next check-in. If you arrive and assess the property needs more work than the time allows — contact Bonnie before starting. Never rush and cut corners. Call first.

What makes a new build clean different

Construction and renovation sites leave specific residues not found in standard residential cleans: silica dust, plaster dust, grout haze, paint splatter, adhesive residue, silicone smears, and protective stickers on glass and fixtures.

The safety requirements and removal techniques are significantly different from a bond clean.

Mandatory requirements before starting any new build

SWMS read and signed before startingConstruction sites are high-risk work environments. Legal requirement — no exceptions.
P2 mask — when dust is actively airborneMandatory on active construction sites or as soon as you begin disturbing settled dust. Not a surgical mask — P2 rated only.
Safety glasses, gloves, closed-toe non-slip footwearConstruction sites have additional sharp debris hazards.

New build clean — order of operations

1
Full PPE on before entering. SWMS signed.
2
Photograph entire property on arrival
3
HEPA vacuum all surfaces — walls, ceiling, floors, sills, tracks, inside cupboards
The most important step. Do not rush. Thorough HEPA vacuuming dramatically reduces the wet cleaning effort that follows.
4
Remove all protective film from glass, appliances, and fixtures
5
Remove stickers — flat scraper at 0 degrees, surface dampened first
Pro Multi-Purpose on the glass first, then flat scraper. Any angle risks permanently scratching brand new glass.
Pro Multi-Purpose
6
Remove grout haze from tiles
Appropriate grout haze remover confirmed by Bonnie. Work in sections.
7
Remove paint splatter — flat scraper on glass (wet, 0 degrees), appropriate solvent elsewhere
8
Room by room wet clean — same process as bond clean
9
Windows inside and out — streak-free
Pro Multi-Purpose
10
Second HEPA vacuum pass — all floors
Picks up dust dislodged during wall and surface cleaning.
11
Mop all hard floors
Multipurpose
✓
Before and after photos for residue removal — sent to Bonnie via WhatsApp

What NOT to do on a new build

Never use microfibre on dusty surfaces firstEmbeds silica particles into the cloth and spreads them. HEPA vacuum first. Always.
Never use a standard vacuumFine silica passes through standard filters and goes back into the air. HEPA vacuum only.
Never angle a scraper on new glass0 degrees, surface dampened first. Any angle risks permanent scratching.
Never use abrasive pads on new tiles or benchtopsNew surfaces scratch easily. Soft cloths only unless specifically approved.

Guest touch points — the surfaces guests physically contact

Airbnb guests notice two things immediately: smell and cleanliness of surfaces they touch. The first thing most guests do when they arrive is touch things — door handles, light switches, taps. If those surfaces feel sticky, marked, or unclean, the property fails the first impression before they've even put their bags down.

Every touch point — sanitise these on every turnover

!
Front door handle and lock mechanism
The first thing every guest touches. Wipe with PRO Multi-Purpose, dry buff. Check the keypad or lockbox is clean and working if applicable.
!
All light switches — every room
Finger marks accumulate on switches over dozens of stays. PRO Multi-Purpose on a microfibre, wipe each switch and the wall immediately around it. Every switch, every room.
!
TV remote
One of the most touched and least cleaned items in any short-stay property. Wipe with PRO Multi-Purpose. Check batteries still work — if they're flat, notify Bonnie and the host via the group chat.
!
All tap handles — bathroom and kitchen
Taps are touched with wet or soapy hands constantly. Water marks, soap residue, and finger marks all accumulate. PRO Bathroom on bathroom taps, PRO Multi-Purpose on kitchen. Polish dry — no water marks left.
!
Toilet flush button or handle
Every guest, every visit. PRO Bathroom and Toilet, clean and dry. Check under the rim has been treated (apply on arrival to dwell).
!
Fridge door handle and door seal
Handle gets touched constantly. The door seal collects food debris and moisture — check and wipe it. Inside the fridge: remove any food left by previous guests, wipe shelves.
!
Kettle and coffee machine handles
Touched every morning. Wipe down exterior with PRO Multi-Purpose. Check the kettle has been descaled recently — if there's visible build-up inside, note it to Bonnie.
!
Stair rail and balcony rail
Every guest who uses the stairs touches the rail. Hand grease and marks build up quickly. Wipe with PRO Multi-Purpose, dry immediately.
The touch point test: Before you leave any Airbnb, physically touch each of these yourself. If it feels clean to you, it'll feel clean to the guest. If anything feels tacky, marked, or rough — go back and fix it.

The kitchen — the #2 and #3 review complaints

According to Bonnie's experience, the top review complaints from Airbnb guests are: 1. bed presentation, 2. dirty sinks or benches, 3. dirty cutlery, glasses, or bins not emptied.

The kitchen and dining area covers two of the top three. This is where your attention to detail directly affects the host's income from reviews.

Kitchen specifics — go through every one

!
All cutlery, glasses, and crockery — washed and polished
Previous guests may have run the dishwasher but not unpacked it, or hand-washed items poorly. Check every item. A glass with lipstick, a fork with food residue, or a mug with tea stains is an instant 1-star comment. Wash, rinse, dry with a clean cloth, check against the light before putting away.
!
Sink — clean, dry, no food debris in drain
The sink is one of the first things guests look at. Remove drain debris, scrub the sink basin, clean the tap, dry the whole sink completely. A wet, marked sink after a clean looks like it wasn't cleaned.
!
Bins — emptied and relined, every single bin in the property
Not just the kitchen bin. Bathroom bins, bedroom bins, any bin in the property. Empty, wipe the inside of the bin if needed, fresh liner. A bin that wasn't emptied is a cleanliness failure a guest will mention by name in a review.
✓
Benchtops — clear, streak-free, dry
Everything off the bench that shouldn't be there. PRO Multi-Purpose, wipe, dry buff. No crumbs, no marks, no water streaks. Check from the side at eye level — this is how guests look at benchtops.
✓
Microwave — inside and out
Splatter inside the microwave is common and always noticed. Wipe with PRO Multi-Purpose inside and out. Check the turntable plate is clean.
✓
Stovetop and rangehood filter
PRO Degreaser on the stovetop if there's visible grease. Rangehood filter — remove and check. If heavily soiled, notify Bonnie. Light soiling — wipe with PRO Degreaser.

Consumables — checking and notifying

You are not responsible for purchasing consumables — but you are responsible for notifying Bonnie and the host when supplies are running low. This is done via the group chat that includes Bonnie, you, and the Airbnb host or manager.
Toilet paper — check all bathrooms. Minimum 1 full roll per bathroom plus 1 spare visible. If running low: notify in group chat before leaving.
Coffee and tea — check host supply. If less than 2 servings remaining: notify group chat.
Milk — if host provides milk, check the date and quantity. Expired milk must be removed and host notified.
Soap and hand wash — check pump level. If less than ¼ full: notify group chat.
Dishwashing liquid and sponge — check level and condition. A sponge that smells or looks worn reflects on the property.
Never purchase consumables without host approval — your role is to notify, not to spend money on behalf of the host. Message the group chat and let them direct you.
The group chat rule: Every Airbnb job has a WhatsApp group with you, Bonnie, and the host or property manager. Any consumable issue, any damage, any question about the property — goes in the group chat. Never contact the host directly outside the group. Never make decisions about the property without Bonnie knowing.

Finding damage or missing items

Guests occasionally break things, leave things behind, or remove items from the property. Finding damage or a missing item is not a disaster — it is information the host needs to act on. Your job is to document it immediately and notify the group. Nothing more, nothing less.

Exactly what to do — step by step

1
Stop — do not move or attempt to clean the damaged item
If you find broken glass, a damaged surface, or a stain that may be significant — stop immediately. Do not move it. Do not clean around it before photographing. The evidence needs to be photographed in the state you found it.
2
Photograph — clearly, from multiple angles
Close-up to show the damage detail. Wide shot to show the location in the room. If something is missing — photograph the empty space where it should be (e.g. the empty TV bracket, the empty towel rail).
3
Post to the group chat immediately — with a factual description
The group chat has you, Bonnie, and the host or property manager. Post your photos with a short, factual description: "Found a cracked tile in bathroom — photo attached" or "TV remote is missing from the bedroom." Do not speculate about how it happened. Do not blame the guests in the message. Facts only.
4
Wait for direction from Bonnie before proceeding
For anything significant — damaged furniture, broken appliances, large stains — wait for Bonnie's response before continuing. For minor damage that doesn't affect cleanliness, continue cleaning after documenting.
5
Never make assumptions about the guest
Your job is to document, not to investigate. "Looks like guests had a party" or "they clearly didn't care" are not professional observations and are not appropriate for a group chat the host can see. Document the facts. Let Bonnie and the host make their own assessment.

The time pressure reality

Airbnb turnovers are often under real time pressure — sometimes 2–3 hours between checkout and the next check-in. Finding significant damage changes the picture. If the damage or condition of the property means you cannot complete the turnover to standard in the time available — tell Bonnie immediately. Do not rush and cut corners. The host would rather know the situation and manage the guest's expectations than have a new guest check in to a half-cleaned property.

What a 5-star Airbnb review actually requires

Guests do not leave 5-star reviews for clean properties. They leave 5-star reviews for properties that felt like nobody had ever stayed there before. That is the standard you are working to — not "clean" but "brand new feeling."
Understand the guest mindset. Guests are paying more per night than most hotels. They have expectations that match that price. One hair on a pillow, one smear on a mirror, one sticky spot on the stovetop — and the review drops. They notice everything because they are paying for perfection.
1
The bed is everything
Fresh linen, straight and tight — hospital corners if possible. Pillows plumped and centred. No wrinkles, no hair, no smell. A guest forms their entire impression of the property the moment they walk into the bedroom. Get the bed perfect first.
2
The bathroom needs to sparkle — not just be clean
Streak-free mirrors. No water marks on taps or glass screens. Fresh towels folded with a neat edge. Toilet paper with a pointed fold at the end. Guests compare this to hotel standards — meet them.
3
Smell is the first thing guests register
The property needs to smell clean and fresh — not of cleaning products. Ventilate properly. Empty all bins. Check for mould or damp smell in bathrooms. A property that smells slightly off will get a lower review regardless of how it looks.
4
Reset everything to a hotel-room standard
Remotes placed neatly. TV guide or welcome folder straight. Cushions symmetrical. Coffee pods counted and replenished. Toilet roll replaced. Every visible item placed deliberately — not just left where the last guest put it.
5
The kitchen must look unused
Stovetop spotless. Inside the microwave clean. No water marks in the sink. Dish rack empty and clean. Benches completely clear and wiped. A guest should open the kitchen and feel like they are the first person to use it.

Common guest complaints — and how to prevent them

Hair — the number one Airbnb complaint globally. Check every drain, every pillow, every surface. One hair in the bathroom or on the sheets = 1-star review regardless of everything else.
Smells — musty, smoky, or stale cooking odours. Ventilate properly. Empty all bins completely. Check soft furnishings for absorbed odours.
Dust on hard-to-reach surfaces — ceiling fan blades, top of picture frames, skirting boards. Guests with allergies notice immediately.
Previous guest's belongings — check under beds, in drawers, behind cushions, in wardrobes. Guests finding previous guest's items is an instant 1-star.
Dirty appliances — inside the coffee machine, the toaster, the microwave, the oven. Guests who cook notice immediately if appliances are not clean inside.
The 5-star finishing move — once the clean is done, do a slow walk-through as if you are the guest checking in for the first time. Look at everything from their perspective. If something looks less than perfect — fix it.

Module 9 · New builds & builders cleans

New builds and builders cleans

A builders clean is one of the most demanding jobs in the industry — long hours, hazardous dust, precision detailing, and a client who expects a handover-ready finish. Understanding what a builders clean involves makes you a more complete cleaner.

Module 8 recap3 quick questions before Module 9

A completely different job

A builders clean is not a thorough residential clean — it is a specialist service requiring different products, different PPE, more time, and a completely different approach. Construction residues require specific treatment that standard cleaning products cannot handle.

Key differences from a standard clean

1
The dust is dangerous
Silica dust from cutting tiles, concrete, or stone causes permanent, irreversible lung disease. P2 mask is mandatory when dust is airborne or being disturbed. No exceptions.
2
Everything is a first clean
Cabinetry, appliances, fixtures, and glass have never been cleaned. They may have protective film, adhesive labels, paint overspray, grout haze, and silicone smears on every surface.
3
The time is completely different
A full builders detail clean commonly runs 8–16 hours across one or two days. Always confirm the full scope and time allocation with Bonnie before starting.
4
The standard is handover-ready
The builder is handing this property to the buyer or tenant. Every surface needs to be spotless, every fixture polished, every edge detailed. Presentation-perfect — not just clean.
5
Work top to bottom, room by room, always
Start at the highest point — cornices, fans, high shelving — and work down. Dust falls. Never clean a floor before the surfaces above it are done.
Builders cleans are charged at a higher rate — reflecting the specialist skill, time, and physical demands involved. Doing this work well is a genuine career skill.
WoodBClean new build
New build bathroom — WoodBClean job site. Large format stone tiles, frameless shower screen, polished concrete appearance. Every surface here requires specific product knowledge.
Silica dust causes silicosis — permanent, progressive, and potentially fatal. There is no cure. P2 mask mandatory when dust is airborne. Non-negotiable.

Before you start — mandatory

1
Read and sign the SWMS before starting
Construction sites are high-risk environments. Legal requirement — no exceptions.
2
P2 mask whenever dust is airborne or being disturbed
Not a surgical mask. P2-rated only. On as soon as you begin disturbing settled construction dust.
3
Nitrile gloves for all chemical use and surface work
Construction residue removers are strong chemicals. Full glove coverage throughout.
4
Eye protection when spraying near glass or working overhead
Splashback risk is higher due to the volume of chemical use on builders cleans.
5
Confirm with Bonnie before removing any builder's protective film
Some protective coverings are left intentionally by the builder until the formal handover. Never remove without confirmation.

Why this matters

Silicosis cases in Australia have increased significantly among tradespeople and cleaners in construction environments. Young workers have been diagnosed in their 20s and 30s. The dust is invisible when settled — you cannot judge the risk by what you can see. Wear the P2 mask.
Wall washing is standard on nearly all builders cleans. Unless Bonnie specifically advises that trades were exceptionally clean, assume walls need to be washed — construction dust, handprints, smears and light marks are present on virtually every new build. This is one of the most commonly missed steps.

The builders clean process — step by step

Work top to bottom, room by room. Complete each room fully before moving to the next.
1
Walk the job with the brief
Before touching anything, walk the entire property with the scope of works. Note anything unusual — damage, heavy residue, staining. Photograph and send to Bonnie before starting.
2
Remove all loose debris and rubbish
Builder's offcuts, packaging, tape, cardboard, cable ties. Clear each room before cleaning. Do not assume the builder has removed everything.
3
High dust — ceilings, cornices, fans, high shelving
Extension dusters. Work across the full ceiling and all high surfaces before touching walls. P2 mask on.
4
Walls, skirtings, architraves, door frames, power points
Spot clean marks and dust. Detail work with a damp cloth on all trims, frames, and architraves — construction dust collects in every edge.
5
Glass — windows, frames, sills, tracks
Use specific glass cleaner and a razor blade scraper for dried residue. Polish to streak-free finish. Never use abrasives on glass.
6
Cabinetry — inside and out
Every cupboard and drawer cleaned internally and externally. Remove protective film from hinges and handles. Polish all door faces.
7
Wet areas — bathrooms, laundry, kitchen
Full detail including tiles, grout lines, screens, tracks, tapware, and fixtures. Grout haze requires specific remover — not standard cleaner.
8
Appliances
Clean externally. Oven, stovetop, rangehood cleaned and polished. Remove all stickers and protective film. Check inside ovens and dishwashers for builder's debris.
9
Floors — vacuum first, then mop
Always vacuum before mopping. Use the correct product per floor type. Check compatibility chart. Tile grout lines may need a grout brush. Floor is always last.
10
Final walkthrough — photograph and send to Bonnie
Walk every room. Check glass at an angle for streaks. Check floors at a low angle for dust. Photo every room before leaving.
Photo documentation on builders cleans is mandatory. Before and after every room. These protect you, WoodBClean, and the builder if any dispute arises.

Working as a team — the standard approach

A builders clean is almost always a two-person job or more — except for small renovation cleans. Working in coordinated roles avoids doubling up, saves hours, and produces a cleaner result.
1
Walk the job together before splitting
Both people walk the full property with the brief. Note problem areas, flag anything unusual, photograph anything damaged before you start. Always do this together — two sets of eyes miss less.
2
Remove all debris — both people together
Before any cleaning begins, walk every room and remove all builder's rubbish, offcuts, packaging, and materials. Clear the workspace first. This is always done together — it's faster and safer with two.
3
Split: one person dusts high and surfaces, one vacuums
Person 1 works top to bottom — ceiling dust, cornices, fans, walls, skirtings, window frames. Person 2 follows with the vacuum, picking up everything that falls. Never vacuum after someone is still dusting above you — you'll be vacuuming twice.
4
Split wet areas: one on glass, one in bathrooms/laundry
Glass and windows require focus and time. Assign one person to all internal glass while the other does bathroom and laundry deep cleaning. Switch and check each other's work before moving on.
5
Both on kitchen, then floors last — always together
The kitchen is the most time-intensive area and benefits from two people working through cabinetry, appliances, and benchtops simultaneously. Floors are always the absolute last task — only after every surface above them is completely done.
For small renovation cleans (e.g. one renovated bathroom or a single room), one person may be sufficient. Confirm with Bonnie before every job — she will tell you the team size required.

External works limited to safe and accessible areas only. Never work at height without appropriate equipment and a signed SWMS. Confirm with Bonnie before any roof or ladder access.

Construction residues — what they are and how to treat them

Standard products will not remove most construction residues. Using the wrong product can permanently damage surfaces. When unsure — photograph and call Bonnie.
1
Grout haze on tiles
White cloudy film left after grouting. Use a dedicated grout haze remover — not general cleaner or vinegar. Apply, dwell, agitate with non-scratch pad, rinse thoroughly. Test on a small area first.
2
Adhesive residue and sticker glue
Use citrus-based adhesive remover. Do not use solvents on painted surfaces or plastics. Remove residue then clean surface normally.
3
Paint overspray and splatter
On glass — razor blade scraper at a shallow angle on wet glass. Never dry scrape. On timber — do not use solvents. Report to Bonnie if significant.
4
Silicone smears
Fresh silicone peels with a plastic scraper. Cured silicone requires a silicone remover product. Never use a metal blade on glass shower screens.
5
Concrete and plaster dust on floors
Vacuum first — never wet mop construction dust directly as it turns to paste and can damage grout and floor surfaces. HEPA vacuum if available.
6
Protective film on appliances and glass
Peel carefully from one corner. If adhesive remains, use citrus remover. Never use a blade on stainless steel appliances.
Never improvise products on a builders clean. If you are unsure about a residue or surface, photograph it and call Bonnie. Wrong chemicals on new surfaces can cause permanent damage WoodBClean is liable for.
WoodBClean new build handover
Completed new build — WoodBClean job site. This is what a handover-ready finish looks like. Timber-look LVT floors, feature lighting, high-spec joinery. Every surface in this room was prepared by a WoodBClean team.
WoodBClean new build site
New build with bespoke timber joinery and textured stone wall — high-spec new build requires careful product selection. No acid on the stone, no over-wetting on the timber, plastic scraper only on any silicone excess.

The handover standard

When a builders clean is complete, the property needs to be ready to hand to the buyer or tenant. The standard is not "clean" — it is "impressive."

The self-inspection test

1
Glass — check at an angle in natural light
Streaks are invisible front-on. Look across the glass at an angle. Any streaks = not finished.
2
Floors — check at a low angle with light raking across
Get your head near floor level and look across the surface. Dust and footprints invisible from above become visible from a low angle.
3
Fixtures and tapware — check for fingerprints and water spots
Polish is not complete until the fixture shines with no visible marks. Microfibre final buff on all chrome and stainless.
4
Edges and corners — construction dust hides here
Run a finger along the base of walls, inside corners, and along skirtings. If your finger picks up dust — not finished.
5
Photograph every room before you leave
Wide shot and detail shots. Send to Bonnie. This is your evidence and your standard.
Delivering an excellent builders clean builds a referral pipeline with builders and developers. These clients return for every project. The standard you set on one job creates the next job.
WoodBClean new build site
New build LVT (Luxury Vinyl Tile) flooring being cleaned — wood-grain LVT is one of the most common new build floor types in Queensland. Note the product on the floor — this is what correct application looks like before the mop pass.

The things new build cleaners most commonly miss

Bonnie's experience on builders cleans is clear: the missed items aren't usually the big obvious things — they're the small details that require common sense. Paint overspray on a door frame. Grout residue on tiles. A sticker that wasn't removed. These take 30 seconds each and they're the difference between a handover-ready finish and a callback.

Most commonly missed — go through every one

!
Paint overspray on door frames, skirting boards, and glass
Painters overspray onto adjacent surfaces — it's inevitable on every new build. On glass: soften with water first, then a plastic razor scraper at a low angle. Never metal on glass. On timber frames: a damp cloth while the paint is fresh. Dry paint on timber — PRO Multi-Purpose on a cloth, gentle circular motion. Do not scratch timber with any blade.
!
Grout haze on bathroom and kitchen tiles
New grout leaves a white hazy film on the tile surface — it's not dirt, it's alkaline mineral residue. PRO Shower (acid-based) applied on dwell will dissolve grout haze on ceramic and porcelain tiles. Agitate with a soft nylon scrubber, rinse thoroughly. Never use acid products on natural stone tiles — water only and flag to Bonnie.
!
Stickers and protective film on fixtures and glass
Appliances, tapware, shower screens, mirrors, and windows often have manufacturer stickers and protective film. Peel slowly from a corner — heat with a hairdryer if stubborn. For adhesive residue: citrus-based adhesive remover on a cloth, leave 30 seconds, wipe clean. Confirm with Bonnie before removing any builder's protective film — some is intentional until formal handover.
!
Silicone excess around bath, shower base, and basin
Silicone is applied and inevitably leaves smears on adjacent surfaces. Use a plastic scraper only — never metal. Score along the edge, peel slowly. Residue on tiles: PRO Shower on a cloth, agitate, wipe. Leave silicone bead intact — do not disturb the seal itself, only the excess.
!
Floors — mopped correctly for the surface type
New build floors have grout haze, construction dust, and adhesive residue. Vacuum first — always. Then damp mop only on timber and vinyl. Never wet mop a new build timber floor. Tile floors can take more water but change mop water frequently — construction dust turns mop water grey immediately. If you're mopping grey water across a new floor, you're spreading concrete dust, not cleaning.
!
Inside windowsills and tracks — construction debris
Window tracks on new builds accumulate plaster dust, silicone smears, and construction debris that standard vacuuming misses. Use a small brush to loosen, vacuum, then wipe each track individually with a damp cloth. Check every window.
✓
Exhaust fan covers — remove, wipe, replace
New build exhaust fans have construction dust on the cover and inside. Remove the cover, wipe with PRO Multi-Purpose, vacuum the housing inside, replace.
✓
Light fittings and downlight holes
Plaster dust settles inside and around every light fitting and downlight hole on a new build. Vacuum each one carefully. Wipe the surrounding ceiling plaster. Do not spray product near electrical fittings.
💡
Common sense on a new build: If you see paint overspray on a door frame, grout residue on a tile, or a sticker that was missed — you clean it. You don't walk past it because it wasn't specifically listed. That's what Bonnie means by common sense. The builder and buyer are relying on a handover-ready finish.

Builder communication — this is not your role

On a new build or builders clean job, you are not the client-facing representative of WoodBClean. All communication with the builder, site supervisor, developer, or buyer goes through Bonnie or an appointed WoodBClean supervisor.

This is not because Bonnie doesn't trust you — it is because builder relationships are commercial relationships that require specific knowledge of contracts, scope, and pricing. One misunderstood conversation between a cleaner and a builder can cost WoodBClean a long-term contract.

What this looks like in practice

A builder approaches you on site and asks about the scope or timeline — "That's a question for Bonnie — I'll let her know you want to connect." Then message Bonnie immediately.
A site supervisor asks you to do something outside the agreed scope — "I'll check with Bonnie before I proceed with that." Do not agree to additional work, do not refuse directly. Escalate to Bonnie.
A builder comments on the quality of your work — positively or negatively — acknowledge politely, say nothing further, and let Bonnie know. Both positive feedback and complaints are Bonnie's to manage.
You find something that affects the scope — unusual residue, damage, missing surfaces — photograph, message Bonnie immediately, wait for instruction before proceeding.
Never agree to extra work without Bonnie's authorisation — even if it seems minor. Scope creep on a builders clean can turn a profitable job into an unpaid overtime situation quickly.
Never discuss pricing, timelines, or WoodBClean's other clients with anyone on site — this is commercially sensitive information that is not yours to share.

Your job on site — in plain terms

Arrive. Walk through. Put your head down. Do exceptional work. Photograph your progress and completion. Message Bonnie when done. Leave the site cleaner than you found it and let the work speak for itself.

Bonnie manages the relationship. You manage the clean.

Module 10 · Mould treatment

Mould treatment

Mould is one of the most serious issues you will encounter on a WoodBClean job. This module covers identification, Level 1 treatment, and the pathway for Level 2 remediation — plus a visual guide to recognising mould types in the field.

Module 9 recap3 quick questions before Module 9
Module 8 recap — 3 questions

Mould identification — Level 1 vs Level 2

L1
Level 1 — surface mould (all trained staff can treat)
White, grey, or light black patches on grout, silicone, tiles, or painted surfaces. Isolated spots or streaks. Surface-level only, not penetrating structure. Contained to one area.
L2
Level 2 — stop immediately and call Bonnie
Dark black or greenish-black patches (especially slimy or fuzzy). Mould covering more than 1 square metre. Mould in multiple rooms. Strong pervasive musty smell throughout. Mould appearing to come from inside walls or ceiling.
When in doubt — stop and call Bonnie. You are never expected to make this call alone. Escalating unnecessarily is far better than under-treating a Level 2 situation.
Queensland Health — mould guide Safe Work Australia — mould hazards

Where to check on every job

Shower grout and silicone, bathroom ceiling corners, around window frames and sills, behind and under the toilet, laundry walls, underneath sinks, behind furniture against exterior walls.

4 real scenarios — what would you do?

Scenario 1
You are cleaning a bathroom and notice grey mould on the grout lines in the shower. It covers about 20cm of a single grout line.
Level 1. Photograph, notify Bonnie, then treat with Pro Mould using full PPE. This is surface mould, contained to one small area.
Scenario 2
You arrive at a property and the entire bathroom ceiling is covered in dark black mould. There is a strong musty smell when you walk into the house.
Level 2. Stop immediately. Do not enter the affected area. Call Bonnie straight away. Photograph from a safe distance. Do not attempt to treat this with Pro Mould and standard PPE.
Scenario 3
You find mould on the bathroom ceiling. It is dark coloured but covers only about 15cm in one corner.
Call Bonnie and describe exactly what you see. Dark colour is concerning but the small area could still be Level 1. Bonnie will make the call. Do not proceed until you have spoken with her.
Scenario 4
You find mould in the bathroom, the laundry, and on the bedroom wall behind the bed.
Level 2. Stop and call Bonnie immediately. Mould in multiple rooms is always Level 2 regardless of appearance. Do not treat any of it independently.
Before you touch anything — identify first. The type, size, colour, and location of mould determines whether you treat it (Level 1) or call Bonnie immediately (Level 2). Never guess.

Step 1 — The size rule

Hold an A4 sheet of paper against the affected area. This is your go/no-go test.

📄
Smaller than A4
Level 1 — you can treat this. Follow the L1 protocol with correct PPE.
🚫
Larger than A4
Level 2 — stop. Do not touch it. Photograph and contact Bonnie immediately.
💡
Why A4? Mould coverage larger than A4 usually indicates the spores have penetrated deeper than the surface — meaning surface treatment alone will not solve it and can actually disturb a larger colony into the air.

Step 2 — Colour identification

Colour alone does not determine L1 or L2 — but it tells you what you are dealing with and how to approach it.

Black mould
Most common. Usually Cladosporium or Stachybotrys. Found in bathrooms, around windows, ceiling corners. Can be L1 or L2 depending on size and depth.
Size check critical
Green mould
Often Penicillium or Aspergillus. Common around window frames, on soft furnishings, inside wardrobes. Usually surface-level if caught early.
Often L1 if small
White/cream mould
Early-stage growth or efflorescence (mineral deposits — not mould). Found on grout, concrete, basement walls. Needs careful identification.
Check if it's mould first
Brown/orange mould
Often in bathrooms, under sinks, around dripping taps. Indicates long-term moisture problem. Size test is critical — can spread rapidly.
Check for moisture source

Step 3 — Location tells you the risk

Where mould is found tells you a lot about how serious it might be.

Low risk locations
Surface mould — likely L1
Tile grout · Shower screen corners · Around taps · Window sill edge · Ceiling corner (small spot)
Medium risk — size check critical
Could be L1 or L2
Bathroom ceiling (spread) · Behind toilet · Under vanity · Laundry walls · Wardrobe interior
High risk — contact Bonnie
Likely L2 — do not treat
Behind walls · Under flooring · Roof cavity · Entire ceiling coverage · Any structural surface with visible penetration

Decision tree — what do I do right now?

I can see mould on a surface
Is it larger than an A4 sheet of paper?
YES →
STOP. Do not treat. Do not disturb. Photograph it. Message Bonnie right now with the photo and location. This is Level 2.
NO →
Is it on a hard, non-porous surface (tiles, glass, painted wall)?
YES → Put on PPE. Follow Level 1 protocol.
NO (soft/porous) → Contact Bonnie. Soft materials cannot be surface-treated.

Written reflection — prove you understand

Answer these in your own words before moving on. No multiple choice — write what you actually know.

1. You arrive at a job and find mould on the bathroom wall. Describe exactly what you do — step by step — from the moment you see it until you leave the property.
2. Explain the difference between Level 1 and Level 2 in your own words. What makes something Level 2, and what do you do differently?
3. Why does dwell time matter more than scrubbing harder? Explain it as if you were teaching a new team member.

Level 1 treatment — full process

1
Photograph mould — send to Bonnie before touching
2
Confirm it is Level 1 — if any doubt, call Bonnie
3
Full PPE on — P2 respirator, goggles, disposable gloves, long sleeves
4
Ventilate — open windows, exhaust fan on before starting
5
Apply Pro Mould directly — NEVER dilute, NEVER mix
Allow minimum 5–10 minutes dwell time. Do not wipe yet.
Pro Mould — ready to use only
6
Agitate with stiff grout brush — keep surface wet throughout
Work section by section. Never dry scrub.
7
Wipe with damp microfibre cloths
Used cloths go directly into a sealed bag — never washed with regular laundry.
8
Re-apply if mould persists — more dwell time, not more scrubbing
9
Bag all waste — remove from property
10
Continue standard clean of the area after treatment
✓
Before and after photos sent to Bonnie via WhatsApp

Level 2 — full mould remediation

Restricted to approved staff only. Requires Bonnie authorisation for each specific job. Enter your Level 2 access code.

Incorrect — contact Bonnie for access.
Level 2 restricted content. Only carry out whole-home remediation with explicit Bonnie authorisation for that specific job.

Level 2 PPE — full hazmat

Level 2 remediation process

1
Bonnie authorisation received in writing. SWMS signed. Full hazmat PPE on.
2
Turn off ALL HVAC and fans — cover vents with plastic
Running air systems spread spores throughout the property.
3
Seal all doorways with heavy plastic sheeting and tape
4
Set up HEPA air scrubber inside containment — running continuously
5
Photograph entire site — send to Bonnie before treatment begins
6
Remove and double-bag all infected porous materials
Carefully bagged immediately — do not shake or drag.
7
HEPA vacuum all surfaces — first pass
8
Apply Pro Mould to all hard surfaces — full coverage, 10–15 min dwell
9
Agitate all surfaces — wipe with damp cloths — seal cloths in hazmat bags
10
Second full Pro Mould treatment — dwell, agitate, wipe
11
Second HEPA vacuum pass
12
HEPA air scrubber runs minimum 1 hour after treatment
13
Final inspection photos — send to Bonnie
14
Break containment safely — fold plastic inward, bag all sheeting
15
Doff all PPE in clean zone — into sealed hazmat bags
16
All contaminated waste double-bagged, labelled, disposed per Bonnie instructions

Mould pathway for employees

As a WoodBClean employee, you can be trained and certified to handle Level 1 mould response. This is surface-level mould found during regular cleans — bathrooms, laundries, grout, windowsills, and around plumbing fixtures. You do not need additional qualifications beyond your WoodBClean training to handle Level 1.
L1
What employees can do
Surface mould on tiles, grout, silicone seals, windowsills, walls, and ceilings up to 1 square metre. Standard WoodBClean mould treatment products, P2 mask, gloves, eye protection. This is covered in your Level 1 mould training.
⚠️
What employees must escalate
Any mould area larger than 1 square metre. Any mould inside wall cavities, behind skirting boards, under flooring, or in ceiling space. Any mould with a strong smell indicating deep penetration. Any client or tenant with respiratory conditions. Stop — contact Bonnie immediately.
📈
How employees get Level 2 certified
WoodBClean can sponsor employees toward Level 2 mould remediation certification. This opens up higher-value specialist work, higher pay rates, and the ability to take on full remediation jobs. Talk to Bonnie if this interests you — it is a clear career progression step.
Career pathway: Employee → Level 1 mould certified → Level 2 remediation certification → specialist mould contractor. WoodBClean supports every step of this progression.

Level 2 mould remediation — what subcontractors need to know

Level 2 mould remediation is a specialist service for serious contamination — whole rooms, structural penetration, or properties where the mould has spread beyond surface level. As a subcontractor, you may already hold Level 2 certification, or you may be working toward it. This section covers what Level 2 actually involves and how it works within WoodBClean.

What Level 2 remediation covers

1
Initial assessment and containment setup
Full inspection of the affected area. Identify all contaminated surfaces including hidden areas — wall cavities, subfloor, ceiling space. Set up physical containment using plastic sheeting and negative air pressure to prevent spores spreading to unaffected areas of the property.
2
Full PPE — Level 2 standard
Full Tyvek disposable suit (no skin exposure), P3 half-face respirator or powered air purifying respirator (PAPR), chemical-resistant gloves, eye protection, disposable boot covers. All PPE donned before entering the containment zone. Doffed carefully on exit to avoid cross-contamination.
3
HEPA air filtration running throughout
Commercial HEPA air scrubbers running continuously during all work. This captures airborne spores released during the remediation process. Air is vented to outside where possible. Scrubbers run for a minimum period after work stops before containment is removed.
4
Removal of contaminated materials
Any porous materials that cannot be cleaned — plasterboard, insulation, carpet, timber — must be removed and bagged in sealed heavy-duty plastic. Double-bagged. Labelled as contaminated waste. Disposed of through approved channels. Never taken through unaffected areas of the property unsecured.
5
Treatment of structural surfaces
All remaining structural surfaces treated with antifungal biocide product at correct dilution and dwell time. Applied to surfaces beyond the visible mould zone — mould spreads further than it appears. A second application after drying in severe cases.
6
Clearance testing and documentation
Post-remediation clearance is required before containment is removed and the property is handed back. This may involve air quality testing and surface sampling. Full written report provided to the property owner including before/after photos, products used, and certification of completion.

Whole-home remediation — scope and process

When mould has spread through multiple rooms or systems of a property, whole-home remediation is required. This is one of the most demanding and highest-value services in the cleaning industry.
Residents must vacate for the entire duration of whole-home remediation — typically 3-7 days depending on severity. Pets must also leave. Do not begin work until the property is confirmed vacant.
Work zone by zone — contain, remediate, and clear one zone before moving to the next. Never open containment between zones. Contamination spreads instantly through air movement.
Address the moisture source first — mould always comes back if the cause is not fixed. Identify and document the moisture source (leak, condensation, poor ventilation). Inform the property owner in writing before proceeding.
Document everything — photos before, during, and after every stage. Written log of areas treated, products used, dwell times, air readings. This documentation protects you and the client.
Whole-home remediation rates are significantly higher than standard cleaning — reflecting the specialist skills, equipment, PPE, and liability involved. WoodBClean can connect certified Level 2 subcontractors with whole-home remediation work. Talk to Bonnie about your certification status and available jobs.

Getting Level 2 certified as a subcontractor

If you are not yet Level 2 certified, WoodBClean actively supports subcontractors who want to get there. Level 2 certification opens up a completely different tier of work — higher rates, specialist jobs, and government contracts.
IICRC mould remediation certification Safe Work Australia — mould hazards
Talk to Bonnie about WoodBClean support for subcontractors working toward Level 2 certification. We can connect you with training providers and may be able to assist with costs for the right candidates.

Ventilation during mould treatment — not optional

PRO Mould is effective precisely because it is strong. That means proper ventilation isn't a courtesy — it's a safety requirement. Treating mould in a sealed space concentrates fumes to a level that causes respiratory irritation and can be genuinely harmful with repeated exposure.

Before you apply any mould product

1
Open every window in the affected room
Before you touch the bottle. Cross-ventilation is best — open window plus door to create airflow. If the room has no window (some bathrooms don't), leave the door open and create airflow from an adjacent room.
2
Turn the exhaust fan on
If the room has an exhaust fan — on before you start, on for the entire treatment, and for at least 20 minutes after you finish. The fan is moving contaminated air out. Use it.
3
PPE on before applying product
Gloves on. If you have respiratory sensitivity or you're treating a significant area — P2 mask. PRO Mould should not be inhaled. The dwell time means the product is off-gassing into the room air for 5–15 minutes. Be protected.
4
Client should not re-enter the treated room for at least 30 minutes
Tell the client this before you start — not after. "I'm going to treat the mould in the bathroom now. I'll need you to avoid that room for about half an hour while the product works and the room airs out. Is that okay?"
5
If you feel unwell — stop immediately
Dizziness, burning throat, lightheadedness — leave the space. Get fresh air. Contact Bonnie. Do not push through chemical exposure symptoms. This is what happened at WoodBClean with bleach — the same principle applies here. PRO Mould is safer than bleach but it is still a chemical in an enclosed space.
Never apply PRO Mould in an enclosed, unventilated space. Window open, fan on, door open. Every time. This protects you, the client, and any pets in the home.

Mould is an emotional topic — handle it with care

For many clients, finding mould in their home is a source of genuine embarrassment and worry. They may feel they've failed to keep their home clean. They may be concerned about their family's health. They may be stressed about cost or structural damage.

Your role in this situation is not to diagnose, not to advise, and not to make the situation worse. It is to be calm, warm, and reassuring — and to let WoodBClean's professional follow-up process do the rest.

What Bonnie wants you to say — in your own warm words

If a client is visibly embarrassed or distressed about the mould:
The approach
Reassure them immediately — calmly and warmly. Something like: "This is really common in Queensland with the humidity — we see this all the time. Please don't worry. The treatment we use is known to last two or more years, and we'll get your home sorted. You're welcome to go and grab a coffee or go for a drive — everything will be looking great when you get back."
If they're worried about soft furnishings, the smell, or other areas: "WoodBClean will get it sorted — you'll have a nice clean home when you return. If there's anything else I notice while I'm working, I'll let Bonnie know and she'll be in touch."
Calm voice, genuine empathy — don't rush past their concern. Acknowledge it briefly before moving to reassurance.
Offer them a way out — invite them to leave for a bit. Most clients are relieved to not have to watch. It also means you can work uninterrupted.
Two-year treatment life — this is genuinely reassuring information. Share it naturally, not as a sales pitch.
Never suggest the mould is their fault — not even indirectly. "You should run your exhaust fan more" is not your conversation. That comes in the WoodBClean follow-up email.
Never say "this is bad" or "that won't come out" — these are Bonnie's conversations. If you're uncertain about treatability, say "I'll let Bonnie know and she'll be in touch" and move on.
Never give prevention advice on the job — WoodBClean sends a professional follow-up email to every mould client after the job. That email outlines what was completed, what was treated, and any recommendations including referrals for underlying issues. Prevention advice is Bonnie's domain — your job is the treatment.

The WoodBClean mould follow-up email

After every mould treatment job, Bonnie sends a written follow-up to the client covering: what areas were treated, the products used, the expected treatment life, and any recommendations — including referrals for underlying issues like water leaks or structural moisture that are beyond the scope of surface treatment.

This is the professional, written record of the work. It protects WoodBClean and gives the client confidence. Your job is the treatment — Bonnie's job is the follow-up communication.
If a client asks for advice about preventing mould coming back — tell them warmly: "Bonnie will send you through some information after the job — it covers all the recommendations." That's all you need to say.
