Module 11 · Driving & vehicle safety

Driving and vehicle safety

Every time you travel to or from a WoodBClean job you are representing the business. These are the rules that keep you, other road users, and WoodBClean protected.

Module 10 recap3 quick questions before Module 10

You represent WoodBClean on the road

When you are travelling to or from a WoodBClean job, you represent our brand. Clients, agents, and the public can see how you drive and behave. Your conduct on the road is part of our professional reputation.

Driving rules

Leave on time — never speed to make up for a late startAllow travel time so you are never rushing to a job.
Park legally and considerately at every siteNever block a client driveway, a neighbour driveway, or a fire hydrant — even briefly.
Lock your vehicle when on siteEquipment and products in an unlocked vehicle are a theft risk.
Never use a handheld phone while driving — illegal in QueenslandSignificant fines and demerit points. Pull over safely if you need to make or receive a call.
Never drive when fatiguedAs dangerous as drink driving. Contact Bonnie if you are too tired to drive safely.
Zero tolerance — driving under the influenceAny staff member driving to or from a WoodBClean job under the influence will be immediately stood down.

Pre-drive check — before every trip

Queensland road safety DriveWell Queensland

Journey planning

Employees: Allow enough travel time so you never need to speed. Factor in traffic, school zones, and parking before leaving. If you realise you will be late — call Bonnie straight away, not when you arrive.
Subcontractors: Before every job, confirm your start time in writing with Bonnie. Plan your route in advance and allow buffer time. Arriving late to a client property reflects directly on WoodBClean.
Never guess at a job address — confirm it the night before or first thing in the morning. Save it to Maps and check for traffic before you leave.

Before you leave

Job address confirmed and loaded into Maps
Departure time allows for traffic and parking
Start time confirmed with Bonnie if subcontractor
Equipment and chemicals loaded and secured
Feeling rested and fit to drive

Your vehicle is a work vehicle on every WoodBClean job

Everything in your vehicle must be secured before you drive. A sudden stop can turn a loose bottle of chemical into a serious hazard — for you, your vehicle, and anyone nearby.

Chemical bottles and cleaning products

All bottles upright and secured — in a crate or box, not rolling loose in the boot
All lids tightly closed — check before loading every single time
Never transport chemicals in the passenger cabin — always in the boot or tray, with ventilation
Never leave chemicals in a hot locked vehicle — heat pressurises containers and creates explosion risk
SDS sheets accessible for all products on board

Equipment and loose items

Vacuum and its cord — coiled and stored flat, not trailing out of a bag or tangled around other items
Mop handles, broom handles — laid flat, not propped vertically where they can fall forward
Bags and kit boxes — zip closed and placed so they cannot slide during braking
No loose items on seats or the dashboard — anything unsecured becomes a projectile in a crash
Boot organised — heavier items at the bottom, lighter items on top

Vehicle security

Lock your vehicle every time you leave it — even for one minute. Equipment and chemicals left in an unlocked vehicle are a theft and liability risk.

Setting up for a safe drive — before you start the engine

A distracted or uncomfortable driver is a dangerous driver. Every time you get into the vehicle before a job, take 60 seconds to set up properly. This is not optional — it protects you, your passengers, other road users, and WoodBClean's equipment.
1
Seating position — spine supported, arms slightly bent
Adjust your seat so your back is fully against the backrest and your knees are slightly bent with feet flat on the pedals. Your arms should have a slight bend at the elbows when holding the wheel at 9 and 3. Reaching strains your back over a long day. Sitting too close is a safety risk if the airbag deploys.
2
Drink bottle — in the cup holder, always
Your water bottle lives in the cup holder — not on the passenger seat, not on the floor, not rolling around in the back. If it falls and rolls under a pedal while you're driving, it is a serious safety hazard. Always secured, always within reach without looking down.
3
Bag or purse — back seat floor or passenger footwell, never the driver footwell
Bags on the driver's floor are an entanglement risk with the pedals. Bags on the passenger seat can become a projectile in a sudden stop. Place your bag on the rear seat floor or the passenger footwell. Secure it so it doesn't slide.
4
Phone — mounted or silent, never held
Your phone must be in a mount if you're using it for navigation, or on silent in your bag. Holding a phone while driving is illegal and a $1,000+ fine in Queensland. Using it at a red light is also illegal. If you need to respond to a message — pull over safely first.
5
Loose equipment — secured in the boot or back seat
Vacuum heads, mop handles, spray bottles and buckets must be secured before driving. A loose vacuum head on the back seat becomes a dangerous projectile at 60km/h. Pack the boot or back seat tightly. Heavy items on the floor, light items on top.
6
Mirrors and seatbelt — every trip, no exceptions
Check your mirrors every time you sit down, even if you were the last person in the vehicle. Adjust if anything has shifted. Seatbelt before the engine starts — not at the end of the driveway.
Any accident, near miss or damage to the vehicle or equipment must be reported to Bonnie immediately — same day, not next day. Even minor scratches to equipment or the vehicle must be reported. Attempting to hide damage makes the situation significantly worse.
Employees: You will only carry chemicals in your vehicle when Bonnie specifically assigns you a job that requires it. This is not your regular setup — Bonnie will brief you on what to carry and how before that job.
Subcontractors: You regularly carry a full chemical kit. These rules apply every time your vehicle is loaded.

Transporting cleaning products safely

All bottles upright and secured in a crate or boxNever loose in the boot. A tipping bottle is a chemical spill incident.
All lids tightly closed — check before loading
SDS accessible for all products on boardDigital copies on your phone are acceptable. Emergency services may ask for these.
Spill kit in the vehicle at all timesAbsorbent cloths, disposable gloves, sealed bags, small bottle of water, SDS copies.
Never leave chemicals in a hot locked vehicleHeat can pressurise containers. Remove or shade products.
All bottles correctly labelled — never transport unlabelled bottles

If you are in a road accident

1
Stop immediately — never leave the scene
Leaving the scene of an accident is a serious criminal offence in Queensland.
2
Check for injuries — call 000 if anyone is hurt
Safety first. Everything else is secondary.
3
Move vehicles if safe — hazard lights on
4
Exchange details with other parties
Name, address, phone, licence, registration, and insurance details.
5
Photograph everything before vehicles are moved if possible
Both vehicles, positions, damage, road conditions, signage.
6
Call Bonnie immediately — even for a minor incident
7
Complete a WHS incident report the same day

Your vehicle is part of your professional kit — treat it that way

Bonnie has seen it all. Cleaners speeding to make up for a late start. A vehicle that hadn't been serviced breaking down on the way to a job. A blown tyre that wasn't reported, wasn't noticed, and could have ended far worse. A car so overloaded with unsecured equipment that a sudden stop would have been dangerous.

Your vehicle is not just transport. It is part of your professional operation. If it fails, the job fails. If it's unsafe, you are unsafe.

Basic maintenance — your responsibility as a subcontractor

You do not need to be a mechanic. You need to be a professional who takes basic care of their vehicle. These are the minimums:
1
Tyres — check monthly and before long trips
Check tyre pressure monthly — correct pressure is on the sticker inside the driver's door. Visually check for bulges, cuts, or excessive wear weekly. A blowout on the M1 with a boot full of chemicals is a serious accident waiting to happen. A tyre issue on the way to or from a job — contact Bonnie immediately. Do not drive on a damaged tyre.
2
Servicing — follow your manufacturer's schedule
A vehicle that hasn't been serviced will eventually fail. It usually fails at the worst time — on the way to a job. A $400 service is far less expensive than a breakdown, a tow truck, a missed job, and an angry client. Keep your log book up to date.
3
Registration and CTP — valid at all times
Driving an unregistered vehicle on a WoodBClean job puts you personally liable for any accident that occurs. No valid rego = no valid insurance = you are personally responsible. Check your rego expiry date and set a reminder two weeks before.
4
Warning lights — act on them immediately
If a warning light comes on in your vehicle — do not ignore it and hope for the best. Look it up, assess the severity, and contact Bonnie if it affects your ability to safely complete a job. Never drive a vehicle with an active engine warning light to a job without getting it checked first.
5
Any vehicle issue — communicate immediately
If your vehicle breaks down, has a flat tyre, or has any issue that affects your ability to get to a job — message Bonnie immediately. Don't wait until the job start time. Don't hope you'll figure it out. Early communication gives Bonnie time to arrange an alternative. Late or no communication leaves a client sitting at an empty property.
⚠️
Real situations at WoodBClean: A cleaner was speeding to make a job on time after a late start — this is how serious accidents happen and how WoodBClean's reputation gets attached to a road incident. Another had major mechanical failure because the car hadn't been serviced. A blown tyre wasn't reported to Bonnie. None of these are acceptable. Your vehicle, your responsibility.

Fatigue, drugs and alcohol — zero tolerance, no exceptions

Bonnie includes this section because she thinks it's important — not because she expects the worst from her team, but because these are real causes of real accidents, and real conversations that have to be had in any professional workplace.

WoodBClean has zero tolerance for driving to, from, or between jobs under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or in a state of dangerous fatigue. This is not negotiable and it applies equally to employees and subcontractors.

Fatigue — as dangerous as drink driving

The NSW Centre for Road Safety found that being awake for 17 hours impairs driving performance to the same level as a 0.05 blood alcohol reading. Being awake for 24 hours equals 0.10 — over the legal limit.

Early morning starts are common at WoodBClean. Queensland summer heat adds to fatigue on long jobs. Here's what Bonnie needs you to know:
If you are too tired to drive safely — contact Bonnie before you start the car. Not when you're halfway there. Before you leave.
Signs you should not drive: heavy eyelids, missing turns you know well, not remembering the last few minutes of driving, nodding off at red lights. Any of these — pull over safely, call Bonnie.
You will not lose the job for being honest about fatigue. Bonnie would rather rearrange a job than receive a call from a hospital.
Never push through dangerous fatigue to make a job. The job can be rescheduled. An accident cannot be undone.

Alcohol and drugs — the policy is simple

Zero blood alcohol while driving to, from, or between any WoodBClean job. Not 0.05. Zero. You are in a work vehicle, on work time, representing WoodBClean.
No illegal drug use before or during any WoodBClean job. If a random drug test were conducted at a client site — and some commercial sites do conduct them — a positive result ends the working relationship immediately and may have legal consequences for you personally.
Prescription medications that affect driving: if your medication warns against operating heavy machinery or driving — you must tell Bonnie before accepting driving-involved jobs. This is for your protection and everyone else's.
If you've had a big night and you're not confident driving safely the next morning — tell Bonnie. It is a conversation. It is not the end of your working relationship. Honesty is always the right call.
Any staff member driving to or from a WoodBClean job under the influence of alcohol or drugs will be immediately stood down. This is not a warning — it is the outcome. Bonnie's priority is always the safety of her team, her clients, and the public.

Written reflections — Module 11

These questions are about the judgement calls that keep you and everyone around you safe.

1. It's 6am. You're on the way to a 7am bond clean and you get a flat tyre. Walk through exactly what you do — step by step — from the moment you realise it to when the situation is resolved.
2. You had a late night and got about 4 hours of sleep. You have a job starting at 7:30am. You feel okay — a bit tired but functional. What do you do?
3. You have a minor bingle in a car park at a client's apartment complex while arriving for a job. The other car has a small scratch. What do you do — in order?
4. In your own words — why does speeding to make up time on the way to a job create a bigger problem than arriving slightly late? What's the right approach when you realise you're going to be late?

Professional client communication

What never to discuss with clients

Social media — always

Handling complaints — 5-step process

1
Listen completely without interrupting
Let them finish. Do not get defensive. Do not explain yourself yet. Just listen.
2
Acknowledge — Thank you for letting me know
You do not have to agree with them. Acknowledging is not admitting fault — it is professional.
3
Assess — can you fix it right now?
If it is something small you can fix immediately — do it. Then check: Is that better for you?
4
For anything significant — I will pass this to Bonnie who will contact you today
Then contact Bonnie immediately with full details and your photos.
5
Never argue — never promise — never make decisions above your authority
Even if the client is wrong. Even if you have photos proving it. Stay calm, stay professional, and let Bonnie handle it.

Real complaint scenarios

Scenario 1 — After hours call
It is 7pm and a real estate agent calls to say the oven was not cleaned properly and the tenant has failed their inspection.
Do not argue or get defensive. Thank the agent for letting you know. Tell them you will contact Bonnie immediately and she will be in touch to arrange a resolution. Call Bonnie right away with all your job photos. Your oven photos are your defence.
Scenario 2 — Damage claim
A client calls the next day saying a vase was broken during the clean. You do not recall breaking anything.
Do not argue or deny. Tell them you will pass this to Bonnie immediately. Contact Bonnie with your arrival photos — if the vase was already damaged, your photos show it. If you did break it and forgot to report it — that is now a more serious problem than the original breakage. Always report damage same day.
Non-negotiable
Photos before and after every bond clean are not optional. Without arrival photos, you cannot prove pre-existing damage. Without completion photos, you cannot prove the standard you achieved. Both protect you from claims that could cost you hundreds of dollars.
Scenario 3 — Private discount request
A client you have cleaned for several times approaches you and says they would love to book you privately for half the price.
Decline professionally. That is very kind, but I only work through WoodBClean. Then notify Bonnie the same day. This is a non-solicitation situation — Bonnie needs to know regardless.

The quality self-inspection — non-negotiable before leaving

1
Tops of doors, door frames, and light fittings
The most commonly missed areas. Agents check these first.
2
Ceiling fans — top and underside of blades
Dust accumulates on top of blades and is invisible from below.
3
Skirting boards — all the way around every room
Get to skirting board level to check. Do not rely on a standing glance.
4
All glass, windows, and mirrors — streak-free from every angle
Check in natural light from multiple angles. Tilt to catch reflections.
5
No product residue anywhere
White residue means the surface was not rinsed. Re-wipe with a damp cloth.
6
Every bin emptied and relined
Every room — kitchen, bathrooms, bedrooms, study.
7
Floors — dry, no streaks, no footprints
8
The final question — would I be happy coming home to this?
If the answer is no anywhere — fix it before you leave.

WhatsApp message templates — copy and use

Professional communication is part of the job. These templates cover the most common situations you will face. Copy, adapt slightly to fit the situation, and send. Always keep messages polite, brief, and professional.
Arrival message
"Hi [Client name], this is [Your name] from WoodBClean. I've just arrived at the property and am getting started now. I'll send you a message when I'm done. Please let me know if you have any specific requests for today."
Completion message
"Hi [Client name], just finished up at the property. Everything has been cleaned to the full WoodBClean standard. [Add any specific notes if needed, e.g. 'I noticed the bathroom exhaust fan is quite dusty — I've cleaned it but it may be worth having it serviced.']. Let me know if you have any questions at all."
Damage or pre-existing issue found
"Hi [Client name], I wanted to let you know I've noticed [describe issue clearly, e.g. 'a crack in the bathroom tile near the shower'] at the property. I've photographed it and wanted to flag it with you before I continue. Just want to make sure this is noted so there's no confusion later. Please let me know how you'd like me to proceed."
Running late
"Hi [Client name], I just wanted to give you a heads up that I'm running approximately [X] minutes late today. I'll still complete everything to the full standard — it just means I'll finish around [revised time]. Really sorry for any inconvenience."
Access issue
"Hi [Client name], I'm at the property but I'm having trouble with access — [describe the issue briefly, e.g. 'the key isn't working in the lock' or 'the code isn't working']. Can you please help when you get a chance? I'll wait here for [X] minutes. Thank you."

Scripts for difficult client situations

These situations come up. Having a clear, calm response ready means you never get caught off guard. These are word-for-word scripts — adapt them to your own voice.
1
Client says the clean is not good enough
"I'm really sorry to hear that. I want to make sure you're completely happy with the result. Can you let me know specifically what you'd like me to look at again? I'm happy to come back and address it at no extra charge."

Then contact Bonnie immediately — do not resolve disputes independently.
2
Client accuses you of damaging something
"I take this really seriously and I want to sort it out properly. I did photograph the property before I started — can I send you what I have? I'd also like to loop in Bonnie from WoodBClean so we can work through this together. I want to make sure this gets resolved fairly for everyone."

Always photograph before starting. Always loop in Bonnie. Never admit fault or offer payment independently.
3
Client asks you to do something outside your scope or unsafe
"I appreciate you asking, but that's not something I'm able to do today — it's outside the scope of what I've been booked for [or: it requires specialist equipment]. I'd hate to do it improperly. Can I let Bonnie know and she can arrange the right service for you?"

You always have the right to say no to anything unsafe or out of scope.
4
Client tries to negotiate price on the day
"The price for today's clean was set at booking through WoodBClean — I'm not able to change that on my end. If you'd like to discuss pricing for future bookings, Bonnie is the best person to talk to. I'm happy to pass that along."

Never negotiate prices. Never accept cash payments not arranged through WoodBClean.
5
Client asks you to work directly for them (bypass WoodBClean)
"Thank you — I'm glad you're happy with the work! I'm actually not available for private bookings — all my work comes through WoodBClean. The best thing to do is contact them directly to book again. I'd love to be the one who comes back."

This is a non-solicitation situation. Refer all private booking requests to Bonnie.
Whatever the situation — stay calm, stay polite, and loop in Bonnie. You are never expected to handle difficult situations alone. That is what WoodBClean support is for.

Common sense — the final standard

You've now been through 12 modules. You know chemical safety, equipment, mould identification, bond clean standards, Airbnb protocols, new build technique, and how to handle every situation professionally.

Bonnie's last word on all of it is this: none of it matters if you don't apply common sense in the moment.

Common sense at WoodBClean means: see the full picture, not just the scope. Do the complete job, not just the listed tasks.

What common sense looks like in Module 12 context

1
Clean the whole track — not just the part you can see
Window tracks, sliding door tracks, shower tracks. If you're cleaning a track — you clean the entire length.
Real example
This is the sliding door track Bonnie is talking about. The entire track — corner to corner — must be cleaned. Not just vacuumed across. Use an angled paint brush to loosen debris from each corner, then wipe along the full length.
Both corners. The full run. A track that's 80% clean is not a clean track. Use an angled paint brush or a track brush to get into the corners properly — these are the right tools for the job.
2
If it's dirty — clean it. Even if it's not on the scope
You're cleaning a bond property and you notice the light switch beside the front door is covered in fingermarks. It wasn't on the checklist. Do you clean it? Yes. You clean it. A professional doesn't walk past something dirty because a list didn't mention it.
3
Nothing is left — check everything before you close the door
Before you close a door on a completed room — look at it. Look at the corners. Look at the light fitting. Look at the window sill. Check that nothing has been missed. If you wouldn't be happy arriving to that room as a client — fix it.
4
Use the right tools for the job
An angled paint brush for tight corners and tracks. A track brush for window and door channels. A flat microfibre mop for floors — not a string mop dragged across a new build. The right tool makes the job faster, cleaner, and more professional. If you don't have a tool that's needed — tell Bonnie, and invest in it.
5
Know who you're working for — and work like it
You chose WoodBClean. You've done 12 modules. You know the standards, you know the brand, you know what Bonnie expects. Every job you take carries the WoodBClean name. Work like someone who's proud of that — because by the time you're completing Module 12, you've earned the right to be.
The WoodBClean standard in one sentence: Do the job you'd want done in your own home, with the products you'd want used around your own family, to the standard you'd be proud to show anyone.

Transitioning between job types

A WoodBClean professional doesn't just do one type of job. Over time you'll transition from a bond clean to a new build, from an Airbnb turnover to a mould treatment, from a standard residential to a sellers clean — sometimes in the same week.

Each job type has different priorities, different products, different standards. The skill is switching your mindset — and your kit — to match the job in front of you.

Mindset shifts between job types

B
Bond clean → new build
Bond: you're restoring a lived-in property to a clean standard for inspection. New build: you're doing a first-ever clean of a construction environment. Bond thinking won't prepare you for grout haze, silica dust, and construction residue. Arrive at a new build with the Module 9 mindset — read the environment first, P2 mask ready, plastic scraper in your kit.
A
Airbnb turnover → sellers clean
Airbnb: speed and presentation matter, guest is arriving soon, you have a checklist to execute. Sellers: slow down. The camera is coming. Every reflective surface gets polished twice. These are different gears — don't run a sellers clean at Airbnb pace.
M
Standard residential → mould treatment
Residential: you're cleaning surfaces. Mould: you're treating a health hazard. Different PPE, different products, different communication with the client, and a follow-up process you're not personally responsible for. Read Module 10 before any mould job if you haven't done one recently.
R
Any job → recap Module 6 first
Module 6 is your foundation. Dwell time, room sequence, reading the environment — these apply to every single job type. When in doubt about how to approach any job, Module 6 is your reset point.

Before every job — a 60-second mental checklist

What type of job is this — and what module covers it?
Do I have the right products and PPE for this job type?
What are the specific standards for this job type that differ from my default?
Have I read Bonnie's brief fully — is there anything unusual about this property?
Am I in the right mindset to do this job to WoodBClean standard today?

Specialist Module

Sellers / polish clean

Preparing a property for sale to an elevated finish standard — every reflective surface polished, photo-ready, and presentation-perfect.

What a sellers clean is

A sellers clean prepares a property for sale — for real estate photography and open homes. Same depth as a bond clean with an elevated presentation finish. Every reflective surface must be spotless and streak-free. Real estate photos are often taken immediately after your work.

Key differences from a bond clean

Every reflective surface polished streak-freeGlass, mirrors, taps, tiles, stainless steel — checked from multiple angles in good light.
Final polish pass mandatory in every roomAfter the full clean — a complete second pass on all reflective surfaces before closing the door.
External windows always includedReal estate photos will show streaks on the outside glass.
Pressure washing — only if confirmed by Bonnie before the job
Acid washing for heavy mineral deposits — Bonnie authorisation required. Never proceed without explicit approval.

Sellers clean process

Follow the full bond clean process from start to finish. Then add these sellers-specific steps in every room before closing the door:
+
Polish pass — all glass, mirrors, and stainless streak-free from every angle
Pro Multi-Purpose
+
All taps polished to a shine — no water marks, no fingerprints
+
External windows — glass, frames, sills all completed

Specialist Module

New build cleans

Post-construction cleaning ranges from a single bathroom to a full commercial fit-out. The scope, hazards, process, and standards are completely different at each level. This module covers all of them.

New build cleaning — what it actually means

A new build clean is not a standard clean. Construction leaves behind a completely different type of contamination — silica dust, plaster, grout haze, paint overspray, adhesive residue, concrete splatter, silicone smears, and builder's grime. The goal is not to make a dirty space clean — it is to transform a construction site into a finished, liveable or workable space.

New build cleans are some of the most demanding and highest-value jobs in the cleaning industry. They require patience, the right products, the right process, and an understanding of what "builder's standard" looks like versus "move-in ready."
Bathroom & kitchen
Single wet areas or kitchen fit-outs. Tile haze, silicone, plaster, and builder's dust.
Whole home
Full post-construction clean of a new residential build. Multi-stage, room by room, inside and out.
Commercial & industrial
Offices, retail fit-outs, warehouses, schools, medical centres. Larger scale, different standards, more hazards.
Silica dust is the number one hazard on every new build job. It is invisible, odourless, and causes permanent, irreversible lung damage (silicosis). There is no cure. A P2 respirator is non-negotiable on every new build clean — no exceptions.

Safety requirements — all new build jobs

P2 respirator — must be worn during all dusty work. Not a surgical mask, not a dust mask — a P2 rated respirator. Correctly fitted, covering nose and mouth.
Safety glasses or goggles — construction dust, tile grout haze, and chemical cleaning products are all hazards to eyes. Glasses on before you start.
Chemical-resistant gloves — new build cleaning involves stronger products — tile haze removers, heavy-duty degreasers, concrete dissolver. Gloves appropriate to the chemicals being used.
Steel-capped boots or covered shoes — construction sites have debris, nails, sharp material, and wet concrete. Open-toed shoes are never acceptable on a new build site.
Never dry sweep or dry vacuum silica dust — this launches fine silica particles into the air you breathe. Always wet-suppress dust first, or use a HEPA-rated vacuum. A standard vacuum spreads silica dust — it does not contain it.
Check the site is safe to enter — on new builds, confirm with the builder or site manager that the property is safe and approved for cleaning to begin. Open construction sites can have live electrical, unstable structures, or hazardous materials.

Post-construction bathroom and kitchen clean

Single bathroom or kitchen fit-out cleans are a common entry point for new build work. The space is small but the contamination is concentrated — tile haze across every surface, silicone smears, grout residue, plaster dust, and builder's grime on everything.

Bathroom fit-out — what you are dealing with

1
Tile grout haze
Fresh grout leaves a white hazy film over every tile surface. This must be removed with a pH-appropriate tile haze remover before it fully cures — the longer it is left, the harder it becomes to remove. Work quickly and methodically. Test product in an inconspicuous area first — natural stone requires a different approach.
2
Silicone and sealant smears
Excess silicone around shower screens, bath edges, and wall junctions. Fresh silicone can be carefully scraped with a plastic scraper (never metal on glass or acrylic). Cured silicone requires a silicone remover product. Always work carefully to avoid scratching surfaces.
3
Plaster and paint splatter
Small splatter spots on tiles, fixtures, and glass. Fine plastic scraper or scalpel blade for glass (held at a very low angle). Paint remover for stubborn spots. Never use abrasives on glass or polished surfaces.
4
Fixture and fitting first clean
Tapware, shower heads, toilet suite, towel rails, toilet roll holders — all need their protective film or stickers removed, then polished. Use a soft microfibre — new chrome and brushed nickel scratch easily.
5
Final result standard
Every tile surface streak-free and haze-free. All grout lines clean and visible. Glass and mirrors spotless. All fixtures polished. No construction debris anywhere. Drains cleared. The result should look as though the bathroom has never been used — because it hasn't.

Kitchen fit-out — specific considerations

Splashback tile haze — same process as bathroom tiles. Work quickly before haze cures. Protect bench surfaces with drop cloth while working on splashback.
Cabinetry — wipe all cabinet doors, drawer fronts, and handles. Remove any stickers. Inside all drawers and cupboards — builder often leaves sawdust and debris inside.
Benchtops — identify the surface type first (stone, laminate, timber, Corian) and use the appropriate product. Stone benchtops are often sealed by the builder but confirm before using any acidic product.
Appliances — remove all protective film from ovens, dishwashers, rangehoods, and integrated appliances. Film left on becomes impossible to remove cleanly. Inside of all appliances wiped out.
Never use strong degreasers on new cabinetry paint finishes — new paint is still curing for weeks after application. Harsh chemicals can lift the finish. Use a diluted all-purpose cleaner and soft cloth.

Whole home post-construction clean

A whole home new build clean is a multi-stage job. Construction dust has settled on every surface in every room. Multiple trades have left residue throughout. The property needs to go from construction site to move-in ready — often within a tight timeframe before handover to the owner or tenant.

Whole home new builds can take 1-3 days for a standard residential home depending on size, condition, and number of wet areas. Estimate conservatively — it always takes longer than expected.

Order of attack — whole home new build

1
Builder's inspection first
Walk through the entire property with the builder or site manager before you start. Note any areas of damage, incomplete work, or specific concerns. Document with photos. This protects you — you are not responsible for anything that was already damaged before you arrived.
2
Remove all construction debris and rubbish
Builder is responsible for bulk rubbish removal — but confirm this before you start. Your job begins once the site is clear of major debris. Remove any remaining off-cuts, packaging, and builder's materials before cleaning begins.
3
Top to bottom — ceiling to floor in every room
Start at the ceiling. Cornices, ceiling surfaces, light fittings, exhaust fans. Then walls, window frames, doors and frames, skirting boards. Floors last. Dust falls down — if you clean floors first, you will need to do them again.
4
Wet areas — bathrooms and laundry
All tile haze removal, silicone work, fixture polishing. Each wet area treated as per the bathroom/kitchen process. This is usually the most time-intensive section of a whole home clean.
5
Kitchen
Full kitchen clean including inside all cabinetry, all appliances, benchtops, splashbacks, sink, tapware, rangehood. Remove all protective films.
6
Windows and glass — inside
All interior glass — windows, sliding doors, shower screens, mirrors, glass splashbacks. Streak-free result. Remove any stickers or protective film from glass. Use glass cleaner and a proper window scraper for paint splatter.
7
All floors — vacuum then mop
HEPA vacuum all hard floors first — do not dry sweep silica dust. Then mop with appropriate product for the floor type. Carpet — HEPA vacuum thoroughly. Check for any plaster or paint spots on carpet that need spot treatment.
8
External — garage, alfresco, paths, windows
Garage floor swept and rinsed. Alfresco and entertaining areas. Paths and driveway — pressure wash if required and available. External windows and sliding door tracks. Check gutters for construction debris if accessible.
9
Final walkthrough and handover
Slow, thorough walkthrough of every room. Check corners, behind doors, inside wardrobes, window tracks, skirting boards. Take photos of the completed result. Confirm with the builder or client that the property meets their handover standard.

Commercial and industrial new build cleans

Commercial and industrial post-construction cleans are a different category entirely. The scale is larger, the hazards can be greater, the standards are set by different parties (building owners, tenants, certifiers), and the work often happens under time pressure before a business opens or a lease begins.
Commercial sites may have additional hazards. Heavier construction residue, industrial coatings, epoxy flooring, specialised fit-outs. Always get a full briefing from the builder or project manager before starting any commercial new build clean.

Types of commercial new build clean

🏢
Office fit-out
Partition walls, workstations, glass offices, kitchenette, bathrooms. Heavy dust throughout. Often tight deadline before staff move in. Carpet protection film to be removed from all floors. All glass streak-free — large format glass partitions are a feature, not an afterthought.
🛍️
Retail fit-out
Display cases, shelving, feature walls, lighting fixtures, fitting rooms, service areas. Often high-gloss surfaces that show every mark. Builder frequently installs fixtures close to handover — fresh adhesive, tile work, and paint may still be curing.
🏭
Warehouse / industrial
Concrete floors (often sealed or polished), large open areas, loading docks, amenities blocks. Significant dust load. May require ride-on floor equipment for large floor areas. Confirm equipment requirements before quoting.
🏥
Healthcare / medical centre
Highest standard of all commercial new builds. Clinical-grade finish required. All surfaces must meet infection control standards before any clinical use. Often involves sign-off by an infection control officer. Extra time, extra care, extra documentation.
🏫
School / childcare / gym
High-traffic facilities built to demanding standards. Rubber flooring, commercial carpets, locker rooms, food prep areas, outdoor areas. Often have specific cleaning product requirements due to chemical sensitivities of users.

Key differences on commercial sites

Site induction required — most commercial construction sites require a formal induction before you can work on site. Confirm this with the project manager. Do not arrive on site without knowing what is required.
SWMS required for commercial sites — a Site-Specific Safe Work Method Statement is required for commercial construction sites. WoodBClean will provide this. Read it before you start, sign it, and keep a copy.
Larger equipment may be needed — commercial floor areas may require a ride-on scrubber, pressure washer, or scissor lift for high access. Confirm what equipment is needed and whether it is provided on site or needs to be arranged.
Work in stages if the build is not complete — on large commercial builds, cleaning sometimes begins while construction is still finishing in other areas. Coordinate with the builder to work in completed zones only.
Quoting commercial new builds — commercial new build cleans are quoted separately and are significantly higher than residential. Always contact Bonnie before quoting any commercial post-construction job. Site-specific variables massively affect time and cost.
Commercial and industrial new build cleans are some of the highest-value work available in the cleaning industry. WoodBClean actively pursues these contracts. As a certified, experienced subcontractor, this is a genuine pathway to higher income and more interesting work.

Order of operations — the rule that never changes

On every new build clean, regardless of size — you always work top to bottom, back to front, dry before wet. This is not a preference. It is the only approach that produces a clean result without having to redo work.
1
Dry work first — remove loose dust and debris before any wet cleaning
HEPA vacuum all surfaces before introducing water or cleaning products. Water mixed with construction dust creates a paste that is significantly harder to remove than dry dust. Get the dry dust out first.
2
Ceiling and high surfaces
Cornices, ceiling surfaces, high windows, tops of door frames, exposed beams or steel. Dust settles — work from highest point down.
3
Walls and vertical surfaces
All walls, window reveals, door frames, skirting boards (top and face). Paint splatter, scuff marks, adhesive residue.
4
Fixtures and fittings
Light switches, power points, door handles, tapware, towel rails, appliances. Remove protective films. Polish.
5
Windows and glass
All glass cleaned after walls and frames — not before. Frame cleaning can re-contaminate glass.
6
Floors last — always
Everything above drops onto the floor. Vacuum then mop/scrub when all other surfaces are done. Never clean floors first.

Construction residue — what it is and how to remove it

1
Tile grout haze
White hazy film over tiles from fresh grouting. Use a dedicated tile haze remover — pH matched to the tile type. Acidic remover for standard ceramic and porcelain. pH-neutral for natural stone. Apply, let dwell, scrub with a white pad, rinse thoroughly. Do not let acid-based remover contact grout for extended periods.
2
Plaster and render splatter
Allow to fully dry — do not try to wipe fresh plaster. Once dry, carefully scrape with a plastic scraper. Then clean the residue with warm water and a microfibre. For stubborn dried plaster on glass — a window scraper blade held at a very low angle.
3
Paint overspray and splatter
Fine mist of paint on glass and fixtures from spray painting. On glass — window scraper blade at low angle after softening with warm water. On chrome and fixtures — methylated spirits on a cloth, gently. On painted walls — do not use solvents, use a damp cloth and light pressure.
4
Concrete and screed residue
Concrete haze on tiles, floors, or lower walls. A diluted acid-based cleaner (phosphoric or citric acid) applied with dwell time, then scrubbed and rinsed. Never use on natural stone. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling acid-based cleaners.
5
Adhesive and tape residue
Builders use tape, stickers, and adhesive for protection and marking throughout construction. Remove stickers first. Adhesive residue — eucalyptus oil, lighter fluid, or a dedicated adhesive remover on a cloth. Test on hidden area first. Do not use solvents on fresh paint.
6
Silicone smears and excess
Fresh silicone — plastic scraper, careful. Cured silicone — dedicated silicone remover, let soak, peel away. Never use a metal blade on acrylic, fibreglass, or polished stone. On glass — a sharp blade at very low angle only after the silicone remover has softened it.
When in doubt about a residue type or the right product — contact Bonnie before proceeding. Using the wrong product on a new build surface can cause permanent damage. On a new build, the surfaces are brand new and irreplaceable — one mistake with the wrong chemical can cost thousands.

Mould treatment

Identification, Level 1 surface treatment, and the locked Level 2 remediation module for approved staff.

Level 1 vs Level 2

L1
Level 1 — surface mould — all trained staff can treat
White, grey, or light black on grout, silicone, tiles. Isolated, surface-level, one area, less than 1 square metre.
L2
Level 2 — stop and call Bonnie immediately
Dark black, slimy or fuzzy, more than 1 square metre, multiple rooms, strong musty smell throughout, appearing from inside walls or ceiling.
When in doubt — stop and call Bonnie. Never make this call alone.

Level 1 — 10-step treatment

1
Photograph — send to Bonnie before touching
2
Confirm Level 1 — if any doubt, call Bonnie
3
Full PPE — P2 respirator, goggles, disposable gloves, long sleeves
4
Ventilate — windows open, exhaust fan on
5
Apply Pro Mould — NEVER dilute, 5-10 min dwell
Pro Mould — ready to use only
6
Agitate with stiff grout brush — keep wet
7
Wipe with damp microfibre — into sealed bags immediately
8
Re-apply if mould persists — more dwell, not more force
9
Bag all waste — remove from property
✓
Before and after photos to Bonnie via WhatsApp

Level 2 — full mould remediation

Approved staff only. Requires Bonnie authorisation per job.

Incorrect — contact Bonnie for access.
Only with explicit Bonnie authorisation per job.

Level 2 PPE

Level 2 — 16-step process

1
Bonnie authorisation in writing, SWMS signed, full hazmat PPE on
2
Turn off ALL HVAC and fans — cover all vents with plastic
3
Seal all doorways with heavy plastic sheeting and tape
4
Set up HEPA air scrubber inside containment — running continuously
5
Site photographs — send to Bonnie
6
Remove and double-bag all infected porous materials
7
HEPA vacuum all surfaces — first pass
8
Pro Mould on all hard surfaces — full coverage, 10-15 min dwell
9
Agitate — wipe with damp cloths — seal cloths in hazmat bags
10
Second full Pro Mould treatment
11
Second HEPA vacuum pass
12
HEPA air scrubber runs minimum 1 hour after treatment
13
Final inspection photos — send to Bonnie
14
Break containment — fold plastic inward, bag all sheeting
15
Doff all PPE in clean zone — into sealed hazmat bags
16
All contaminated waste double-bagged, labelled, disposed per Bonnie instructions

Key terms

SDS
Safety Data Sheet
Legal document accompanying every hazardous chemical. Contains hazard information, first aid, PPE requirements, and emergency contact.
SWMS
Safe Work Method Statement
Document identifying high-risk work and required controls. Must be read and signed before starting the identified task.
PPE
Personal Protective Equipment
Gloves, safety glasses, P2 mask, non-slip footwear — any equipment worn to protect against workplace hazards.
GHS
Globally Harmonised System
The international standard for classifying and labelling hazardous chemicals. The 9 hazard symbols are part of GHS.
NES
National Employment Standards
The 11 minimum employment entitlements under the Fair Work Act 2009 that apply to all employees in Australia.
ABN
Australian Business Number
Required for subcontractors to operate and invoice. Register free at abr.business.gov.au.
RSI
Repetitive Strain Injury
Injury to muscles, tendons, or nerves from repetitive movement. Common in cleaning. Managed by alternating hands, taking breaks, and reporting early symptoms.
L1/L2
Level 1 / Level 2 Mould
WoodBClean internal classification. Level 1 — surface mould, treated by all trained staff. Level 2 — structural or whole-home mould, approved staff only.

Your status as a subcontractor

As a WoodBClean subcontractor you operate as an independent contractor. You invoice WoodBClean for your services, manage your own tax and superannuation, and maintain your own insurance. You are responsible for your own financial obligations — WoodBClean does not withhold tax from payments made to you.

Your key obligations

Valid ABNRequired before invoicing. Register at abr.business.gov.au.
Public liability insuranceRequired before commencing work. WoodBClean can assist with guidance on suitable policies.
Submit tax invoices weeklyCovering all jobs completed that week.
Manage your own income tax and superannuationWoodBClean does not do this for you.
Maintain all WoodBClean quality and safety standardsYour contractor status does not change your obligations around PPE, SWMS, and conduct.

Your ABN

An Australian Business Number is required to operate as a contractor and to invoice without having tax withheld at the top rate.

Register free at abr.business.gov.au — takes approximately 10 minutes.

Once registered your ABN must appear on every tax invoice you submit to WoodBClean.

Your tax obligations

Income tax: You must declare all income from WoodBClean in your annual tax return. Set aside approximately 25–30% of your earnings for tax throughout the year.

GST: If your total income from all sources exceeds $75,000 in a year you must register for GST. Below this threshold registration is optional but you may still choose to register.

Superannuation: Generally your own responsibility as a contractor. Check your specific situation with an accountant or the ATO at ato.gov.au.

For tax guidance: ATO at ato.gov.au or contact a registered tax agent.

How to invoice WoodBClean

1
Create your tax invoice at the end of each week
Covering all jobs completed that week. Your invoice must be a valid tax invoice.
2
Your invoice must include
Your name and ABN · WoodBClean as the recipient · Invoice number (sequential) · Invoice date · Description of each job — address, date, hours · Hourly rate and total per job · Total amount (and GST if registered) · Your bank account details for payment
3
Email to woodbclean@gmail.com
4
Payment made within your agreed payment terms

Insurance requirements and recommendations

Public liability insurance — REQUIRED before commencing work
Covers you if a client property is damaged or a third party is injured. WoodBClean can provide guidance on suitable policies — speak with Bonnie before your first job.
Income protection insurance — STRONGLY RECOMMENDED
Covers lost income if you cannot work due to injury or illness. Unlike employees, you are not automatically covered by WorkCover Queensland. Policies from approximately $30–60 per month depending on income.
Vehicle insurance — RECOMMENDED
If using your personal vehicle for work purposes, check your policy covers business use.

Your subcontractor agreement

Your subcontractor agreement with WoodBClean sets out your payment rate, payment terms, availability expectations, insurance requirements, non-solicitation obligations, and termination provisions.

If you have not yet signed your agreement, contact Bonnie before commencing any work. Do not work without a signed agreement in place.

Keep a copy of your signed agreement for your records. If you have any questions about the terms, seek independent advice from the Fair Work Ombudsman (13 13 94) or a legal advisor before signing.
Module 13 · Floors & surfaces

Floors & surfaces — the complete guide

Every floor type you will encounter in the field — timber, vinyl, polished concrete, natural stone, tiles, and carpet. The wrong product on the wrong surface causes irreversible damage. This module means you will never guess.

💡
Did you know?Marble is calcium carbonate — the same mineral as chalk. Acid dissolves calcium carbonate. This is why even a small splash of bathroom cleaner (which is acidic) leaves a permanent dull etch mark on marble that no amount of polishing can fix. Always check the surface before reaching for a product.
Wrong product on wrong surface = immediate callback, potential liability, and a very unhappy client. Five seconds identifying a floor type saves hours of damage control.

Identify before you clean — always

The single most important habit in floor care. Before you apply any product to any floor, identify the surface type. When in doubt — use plain water and a microfibre mop. You cannot damage a floor with water and a clean microfibre mop.

Common floor types you will encounter at WoodBClean jobs:
1
Timber & floating floors
Warm, natural look. Usually has a wood grain texture. Can feel hollow underfoot (floating). Extremely sensitive to moisture and harsh chemicals.
2
Vinyl / LVT (Luxury Vinyl Tile)
Now in 80%+ of new builds. Looks like timber or stone but is plastic. Durable but can be damaged by solvent-based products. Usually has a slight sheen.
3
Polished concrete
Grey, smooth, often reflective. Common in new builds and commercial properties. Acid cleaners will permanently etch the surface.
4
Natural stone — marble, travertine, slate
Often cold to touch, may have visible veining (marble). Very porous, extremely acid-sensitive. One wrong product can cause irreversible etching.
5
Ceramic and porcelain tiles
Most common in bathrooms and kitchens. Durable and versatile. Main challenge is the grout lines, not the tile itself.
6
Carpet
Vacuum only at WoodBClean level. Steam cleaning is a specialist service referred to a carpet professional. Never apply wet product to carpet.
WoodBClean job site
Real WoodBClean job — timber floor with sliding door track. Note how the track crosses the floor — the entire track must be cleaned from end to end, including both corners. This is a common miss on bond cleans.
WoodBClean job site — hardwood timber floor
Polished hardwood timber kitchen floor on a WoodBClean job. Dark timber with visible grain — highly reflective surface. This floor requires a barely damp mop and immediate drying. Even a small puddle left here can cause permanent swelling.

Timber and floating floors

Timber and floating floors are the most common floor type in residential homes — and the most commonly damaged by cleaners who use too much water or the wrong product. Once swelled, warped, or stripped, timber floors cannot be easily restored.
Do: Use a barely damp microfibre mop. Wring out thoroughly — no standing water ever.
Do: Use a pH-neutral timber floor cleaner or Clean Like A Pro multi-surface on a lightly damp mop.
Do: Dry in direction of the boards. Wipe up spills immediately.
Never: Use a wet mop, steam mop, or bucket-and-mop on timber. Water = warping, swelling, mould under boards.
Never: Use vinegar, bleach, ammonia, or citrus-based products. They strip the protective coating permanently.
Never: Use abrasive pads or scrubbers. Scratches timber finish permanently.
The test: If you press your finger to the floor and it comes up wet — your mop is too wet. The floor should dry in under 60 seconds after mopping.
WoodBClean job site — LVT floor
LVT (Luxury Vinyl Tile) flooring on a WoodBClean new build — wood-grain LVT looks almost identical to real timber but behaves very differently. It can handle more moisture than timber but still requires a damp (not wet) mop.

Vinyl and LVT (Luxury Vinyl Tile)

LVT is now the most common flooring in Australian new builds, apartments, and renovated homes. It looks and feels like timber or stone but is actually a multi-layer synthetic product. It is more durable than timber but still has specific needs.
Do: Use a pH-neutral all-purpose cleaner diluted correctly. Clean Like A Pro multi-surface works perfectly.
Do: Damp mop — more water tolerance than timber but not soaking wet.
Do: Vacuum or dry mop first to remove grit before wet mopping. Grit scratches the wear layer.
Never: Use solvent-based products (acetone, turps, petrol-based). Dissolves the wear layer and the adhesive.
Never: Use highly alkaline cleaners or bleach at full concentration. Discolours and degrades the surface over time.
Never: Use abrasive scrubbing pads. LVT wear layer scratches and dulls permanently.
LVT is often mistaken for timber. The difference: timber feels warm and has natural grain variation. LVT feels slightly cooler and has a more uniform, slightly plastic texture. When in doubt — treat it like timber. You cannot over-protect a floor.

Natural stone — marble, travertine, slate

Natural stone is beautiful and expensive — and it is the floor type most frequently damaged by cleaners. The reason: natural stone is acid-sensitive. Even mildly acidic products cause permanent etching that appears as dull spots or white marks that cannot be polished out without professional restoration.
Acidic products that permanently damage natural stone: vinegar, lemon juice, citrus-based cleaners, grout cleaners with acid, bathroom cleaners with acid, some glass cleaners. If a product smells citrus or is labelled "descaler" — keep it off natural stone entirely.
Do: Use only pH-neutral cleaners specifically safe for stone. Check the Clean Like A Pro SDS before applying anything.
Do: Rinse well with clean water after cleaning to remove all product residue.
Do: Dry immediately — water sitting on porous stone causes staining over time.
Never: Use any acidic product — vinegar, citrus, acid-based descalers. One application can cause permanent dull etching.
Never: Use bleach at full concentration on marble or travertine — can cause discolouration.
How to identify natural stone: look for variation in pattern, veining (especially marble), and a slightly cool, heavy feel underfoot. Porcelain can look like marble — porcelain is safe with most cleaners. When unsure — use pH-neutral only and call Bonnie.
WoodBClean job site
Ceramic tiles — large format, light finish. Common in older Queensland homes and bond cleans. Grout lines in these tiles need an angled brush and dwell time. Note the sheen — this surface can handle PRO Shower and general cleaning products.

Tiles and grout

Tiles are generally forgiving surfaces — but grout is porous, stains easily, and harbours mould and bacteria. The grout between tiles is usually where the real cleaning work happens.
Do: Use a tile and grout cleaner or Clean Like A Pro bathroom cleaner. Allow adequate dwell time on grout (2-3 minutes minimum).
Do: Use a grout brush on discoloured grout — agitation is what removes embedded grime, not more chemical.
Do: Rinse thoroughly. Product residue in grout attracts dirt and dulls tiles.
Never: Use acid-based cleaners on natural stone tiles or grout adjacent to stone — check tile type first.
Never: Use metal scrubbing tools on tiles. Scratches glazed surfaces permanently.

Grout cleaning — step by step

1
Apply product directly to grout lines
Spray or pour Clean Like A Pro bathroom cleaner directly onto grout. Work in small sections.
2
Let it dwell — 2 to 5 minutes
Chemistry does the work. Do not scrub immediately. Let the product break down the grime first.
3
Agitate with grout brush
Short back-and-forth strokes along the grout line. Old toothbrush works for tight corners.
4
Rinse thoroughly
Remove all product and loosened grime. Residue left in porous grout attracts more dirt faster.

Surface compatibility quick reference

Use this before applying any product to any surface. When in doubt — pH-neutral only.
Surface Multi-surface Bathroom cleaner Glass cleaner Bleach / disinfectant Degreaser

WoodBClean job site
Outdoor concrete on a WoodBClean job — aggregate finish, expansion joints visible. Sweep first, then damp mop or hose if outdoor. No acid products on plain concrete.

Microcement and polished concrete — the most misunderstood surfaces

Microcement and polished concrete are increasingly common in modern Queensland homes and new builds. They look beautiful, they're durable — and they are extremely easy to damage permanently with the wrong product. Many cleaners mistake them for regular tiles and treat them accordingly. That is a serious mistake.
!
Microcement — never use acid products. Ever.
Microcement is a thin cement-based coating (2–3mm) applied over a substrate. Acid dissolves cement. PRO Shower, vinegar, citrus cleaners, or any acid-based product will permanently etch and discolour microcement. The damage cannot be sanded or polished out. Water and PRO Harmony only — diluted at 1:20.
!
Polished concrete — never use acid or abrasive products
Polished concrete has a sealer on top that gives it the shine. Acid eats the sealer, abrasives scratch the polished surface. PRO Harmony at 1:20, barely damp microfibre mop. If the seal is damaged — flag to Bonnie. Do not attempt to fix it.
✓
How to identify microcement vs regular tiles
Microcement has no grout lines — it's a continuous surface. It may have a slight texture. It often feels slightly cool to touch (like concrete) and can look matte or satin. If you're not sure — ask Bonnie before you use any product. A 30-second question prevents a permanent damage claim.
✓
Outdoor concrete — different rules
Plain outdoor concrete (driveways, paths, patios) can handle more — sweep, damp mop or hose down. PRO Harmony is fine. No acid needed unless there are heavy mineral deposits — and that requires Bonnie approval and specific product.
WoodBClean job site
Dark ceramic grip tiles — small format, matte textured finish with visible grout lines. Typical in laundries, outdoor areas, and some bathrooms. The texture catches debris in every grout line — vacuum before wet cleaning.

Grip tiles and textured surfaces — clean the texture, not just the surface

Grip tiles have a deliberately textured surface for slip resistance. That texture is also very good at trapping dirt, soap scum, grit, and debris. Standard mopping only spreads dirt across the surface — it doesn't lift it out of the texture. These surfaces need a different approach.
1
Vacuum or dry sweep thoroughly first
All loose debris out before any water touches the surface. Wet debris in a textured tile is very difficult to remove — and mopping over dry grit scratches the surface and moves debris rather than removing it.
2
Apply PRO Harmony or PRO Shower with dwell time
Apply product and let it dwell 3–5 minutes. The product needs time to penetrate the texture and loosen dirt that's embedded in the surface. Don't just spray and mop immediately.
3
Scrub with a stiff-bristle brush on heavy soiling
For grip tiles with significant build-up — a stiff nylon brush (not metal) scrubbed in circular motions lifts debris from the texture. A mop alone won't do it. This is the step most cleaners skip.
4
Mop with clean, hot water and change frequently
Grip tiles hold onto dirty mop water. Change your water more frequently than you would on smooth tiles — the texture picks up and re-deposits dirty water quickly.
💡
The grout in grip tiles is often wider and more exposed than smooth tiles. Apply PRO Shower along grout lines with dwell time, then use an angled brush along the grout. Don't skip the grout — it's exactly what an agent or client will look at.

Module 14 · Sustainability

Environmental sustainability and green cleaning

Why eco-conscious cleaning matters, what it means in practice, and how WoodBClean commitment to the environment shapes the way we work.

Why green cleaning matters

Conventional cleaning products contain chemicals that can harm waterways, degrade indoor air quality, and pose health risks to the people who use them every day. As professional cleaners, we use more products more frequently than any household — which means our choices have a significantly greater environmental impact.

Eco-friendly cleaning is no longer a niche preference — it is increasingly required by government contracts, expected by commercial clients, and requested by residential clients. WoodBClean commitment to responsible cleaning is both the right thing to do and a genuine business advantage.
Better for clients: Reduced chemical exposure in their home, safer for children and pets, improved indoor air quality.
Better for you: Lower exposure to harsh chemicals during a working career of repeated use. Fewer respiratory and skin issues over time.
Better for WoodBClean: Required for government and institutional contracts. Differentiates WoodBClean from competitors. Attracts conscious clients.

What makes a cleaning product eco-friendly

Not all products labelled "eco" or "green" are equal. Here is what to look for and what it actually means:
1
Biodegradable surfactants
The cleaning agents break down naturally in waterways instead of persisting in the environment. Look for plant-derived surfactants on the ingredient list.
2
No phosphates
Phosphates cause algae blooms in waterways that deplete oxygen and kill aquatic life. Responsible products exclude them entirely.
3
Concentrated formulas
Less packaging waste, lower transport emissions, lower cost per use. One litre of concentrate can replace 10+ ready-to-use bottles.
4
No artificial fragrance or dye
Synthetic fragrances are common allergens and can affect indoor air quality. Unscented or naturally-scented products are better for sensitive clients.
5
Recyclable or refillable packaging
Trigger spray bottles that can be refilled from concentrate dramatically reduce plastic waste over a working year.
Clean Like A Pro products are concentrated, biodegradable, and designed for professional dilution. Using them correctly — at the right ratio — is already an environmentally responsible choice.

Water conservation in cleaning

Professional cleaning uses significantly more water than household cleaning. Small habit changes across a working week add up to thousands of litres saved per year.
Use microfibre over disposable cloths. A quality microfibre cloth cleans effectively with far less water than cotton cloths or paper towels.
Fill mop buckets to the minimum needed. You rarely need a full bucket. Half-fill, wring thoroughly, refill only when water is visibly dirty.
Turn off taps fully when not in use. A dripping tap wastes 9,000+ litres per year. Check client taps are fully off when you leave.
Use spray bottles instead of soaking surfaces. A targeted spray and dwell time outperforms flooding a surface every time — and uses 90% less water and product.
Allow dwell time to do the work. Proper dwell time means less scrubbing, less repeat application, less water, and better results.

Waste reduction and chemical disposal

How we handle products and waste at the end of a job matters — both for the environment and for safety compliance.
1
Never pour chemicals down storm drains
Storm drains flow directly to waterways — not to treatment facilities. Even diluted cleaning products can harm aquatic environments. Dispose of excess product down a household sink or toilet which connects to the sewage system.
2
Wash microfibre cloths — do not dispose
Quality microfibre cloths last 300+ washes. Washing them correctly (cool water, no fabric softener, air dry) makes them last for years. Disposable wipes are single-use plastic waste.
3
Recycle product containers correctly
Rinse empty spray bottles before recycling. Do not mix chemical residue into recycling. Check your local council's guidelines for chemical containers.
4
Use concentrate and refill
Buying Clean Like A Pro concentrate and refilling trigger spray bottles dramatically reduces plastic waste and cost per clean.

WoodBClean commitment to the environment

WoodBClean is committed to cleaning in a way that is safe for our team, safe for our clients, and responsible toward the environment we all share. This is not a marketing statement — it shapes the products we choose, the training we provide, and the standards we hold ourselves to.
Responsible products
We use concentrated, biodegradable, professionally formulated products. Not the cheapest option — the right option.
Reduced waste
Reusable microfibre, refillable spray bottles, concentrated products. Less packaging in every job.
Water conscious
We train our team to clean effectively with less water — better results, smaller footprint.
Team health first
Products that are safer for our team to use every day, for a full career, without long-term health consequences.

What you actually do — on every single job

Sustainability at WoodBClean is not an abstract value. It shows up in specific decisions you make on every job. None of these slow you down. They are just habits that a professional who cares about their impact forms over time.

The actions

✓
Don't over-spray — two sprays, not five
Every spray beyond what's needed gets rinsed down the drain. Wasted product, wasted chemical, wasted money. Two controlled sprays and dwell time beats five sprays and immediate wiping every time.
✓
Turn the tap off between rinses
Running water while cleaning a different surface is unnecessary. Turn it off. A standard tap runs at 6–12 litres per minute. Over a 4-hour job with careless tap use, the waste adds up significantly.
✓
Change mop water properly — not excessively
Change when grey — not after every swipe. Over-changing wastes water. Under-changing spreads dirt. Change per room on a dirty property, less often on a clean one.
✓
Take your waste with you — don't use the client's bins
Empty product bottles, used packaging, worn cloths — these are your waste. Pack them out in a dedicated waste bag. The client's bins are for the client's rubbish.
✓
Extend the life of your microfibre cloths
Wash correctly, no fabric softener, air dry. A cloth that lasts 200 washes is a fraction of the environmental cost of replacing it every 20. Proper care is sustainability in practice.

Why Australian-made matters — in plain terms

The Clean Like A Pro range is Australian made. When a client asks why WoodBClean doesn't just use cheap supermarket products — here's the answer:

"The products we use are made in Australia by people who understood what professional cleaners actually need. They're more effective at lower dilutions — less product goes down the drain. They're safer for your family and pets. And buying Australian-made supports Australian jobs without shipping chemicals halfway around the world."

You don't need to say all of that. But understanding it means you can answer confidently when it comes up.

Module 15 · Physical wellbeing

Physical wellbeing and long-term career health

Cleaning is physically demanding work. The people who build long, successful careers look after their bodies. This module is WoodBClean saying: we care about you beyond the job.

Your body is your most important tool

A carpenter protects their tools. A chef looks after their knives. As a professional cleaner, your body is your most essential piece of equipment — and the one most people fail to protect.

The physical demands of cleaning — bending, kneeling, overhead work, repetitive wiping, carrying equipment, loading and unloading vehicles — accumulate over time. Small habits practised consistently make the difference between a long, comfortable career and one cut short by preventable injury.
Back injuries are the number one cause of career-ending problems in cleaning. Most are caused by poor lifting technique and repeated awkward bending — both entirely preventable.
Shoulder and wrist injuries from repetitive scrubbing and wiping are the second most common. Technique changes and regular stretching prevent them.
Knee injuries from extended kneeling on hard surfaces are common. Knee pads and correct technique matter.
Report any pain or discomfort to Bonnie early. A small niggle caught early is treated easily. Ignored for months, it becomes a serious injury that sidelines you for weeks. WoodBClean wants you healthy and working for years.

Daily stretch routine — 5 minutes, every day

Do this before starting work and after finishing. Takes 5 minutes. Makes an enormous difference over a working career.
1
Neck rolls — 30 seconds
Slow, gentle half-circles. Left to right. Releases tension from overhead work and driving. Never full circles backwards.
2
Shoulder rolls — 30 seconds
Both shoulders forward 5 times, backward 5 times. Prevents the shoulder tightness that builds from scrubbing and reaching.
3
Wrist circles and finger stretches — 30 seconds
Extend each arm, circle the wrist 5 times each direction. Spread fingers wide, hold 5 seconds. Prevents RSI from spray bottles and scrubbing.
4
Seated or standing forward fold — 30 seconds
Bend forward from the hips, let your upper body hang loose. Knees slightly bent. Decompresses the spine after bending work. Hold, breathe, release slowly.
5
Hip flexor stretch — 30 seconds each side
Step one foot forward into a gentle lunge, lower the back knee toward the floor. Hold. Counteracts the tightness from kneeling and crouching.
6
Calf raises — 20 reps
Hold a wall or bench for balance. Rise onto your toes, lower slowly. Prevents foot and lower leg fatigue from standing on hard floors all day.
Stretching routine for physical workers — before and after work
YouTube · Occupational health stretching

Injury prevention — the habits that matter

Lift correctly, every time. Bend at the knees, not the waist. Keep the load close to your body. Never twist while lifting. Applies to equipment bags, vacuum cleaners, and mop buckets.
Use tools that fit you. Mop handles and squeegees should be at shoulder height when extended. If you are bending your back to mop, the handle is too short.
Swap hands regularly. When wiping large surfaces, switch your leading hand. This distributes strain across both sides of your body.
Wear knee pads for floor-level work. Bathroom grout lines, skirting boards, oven interiors. Ten minutes on hard tiles without knee pads adds up across a career.
Take micro-breaks every 45-60 minutes. Stand up straight, roll your shoulders, take 3 deep breaths, have water. This is not laziness — it is injury prevention.
Never push through sharp or sudden pain. Dull muscle fatigue is normal. Sharp, sudden, or persistent pain is your body signalling damage. Stop and report it.

Hydration and nutrition on the job

Physical work in Australian heat depletes your body faster than desk work. Most fatigue, headaches, and reduced concentration experienced by cleaners in the afternoon is dehydration — not tiredness.
Drink water before you feel thirsty
Thirst means you are already mildly dehydrated. Aim for at least 500ml before starting work, and regular sips throughout the day. In summer, significantly more.
Eat before you start
Physical work on an empty stomach leads to fatigue, poor concentration, and reduced energy. A proper meal 1-2 hours before work makes a measurable difference.
Take your break — it is not optional
A 15-20 minute break mid-job to eat, sit, and recharge is not wasted time. It improves your quality of work in the second half of the job significantly.
Heat awareness in summer
Working in unventilated spaces in Queensland summer is a real heat risk. Know the signs of heat exhaustion — headache, dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating — and stop work, seek shade, and hydrate immediately.

Mental health and working alone

Cleaning is often solo work. You spend hours alone in someone else's space, with no colleagues around. For some people this is peaceful and enjoyable. For others — especially on difficult days — it can feel isolating.

WoodBClean wants to be honest about this: working alone has unique mental health considerations that are rarely talked about in any training program. We are talking about it because we care about every person on this team.
WoodBClean's commitment
Bonnie wants to know if you are struggling — not because it affects the jobs, but because she genuinely cares about the people in her team. A quick message saying "I'm having a rough week" is always welcome. You will never be judged for it.
Connect with the team. WoodBClean is a community. You are not alone even when working alone. Text Bonnie, check in with another team member. Connection matters.
Music, podcasts, and audiobooks make solo work genuinely enjoyable. Many experienced cleaners say this is one of the best parts of the job — uninterrupted time to listen and think.
Notice when you are not okay. Persistent low mood, dreading work, feeling overwhelmed — these are signals worth paying attention to. They deserve the same attention as a physical injury.
Talk to Bonnie. If something at work is affecting your mental health — whether it is a difficult client, a hard situation, or just a rough patch — Bonnie wants to know. Not to judge. To help.
Free mental health support: Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636 · Lifeline 13 11 14 · Head to Health headtohealth.gov.au · All free, confidential, available 24/7.
Beyond Blue Lifeline Head to Health

Body mechanics — task by task

Most cleaning injuries aren't dramatic accidents. They're the result of doing the same movement incorrectly hundreds of times. These are the correct techniques for the tasks you do every day.

Correct technique — each task

V
Vacuuming — stand tall, use the machine's reach
Extend the wand fully. Don't hunch over the vacuum or bend at the waist to reach further. Your back stays straight. Move your feet to reposition rather than reaching from the waist. A backpack vacuum is far better for your spine than an upright — the weight is distributed across your back, not pulled from one arm.
S
Scrubbing bathrooms — kneel, don't bend
Get down to the level of what you're cleaning. Kneeling to scrub a toilet or bath is dramatically better for your lower back than bending over from standing. Use kneeling pads if needed. For lower tiles and grout — a long-handled scrubber keeps you upright.
M
Mopping — handle at shoulder height, let the mop work
The mop handle should be roughly at shoulder height. If you're hunching over the mop, the handle is too short. Let the mop's weight and the figure-8 technique do the work — you should not be pressing hard. Pressing harder does not clean better.
L
Lifting equipment — always use your legs
Feet shoulder-width apart. Bend at the knees, keep your back straight. Hold the load close to your body. Never twist your back while lifting. For heavy equipment — ask for help or use a trolley. One back injury from lifting incorrectly can end a cleaning career.
C
Carrying a caddy — alternate sides, don't overload
A heavy caddy carried on one side every day creates spinal asymmetry and shoulder problems over time. Alternate which hand you carry with. Better yet — use a caddy with a shoulder strap or the Clean Like A Pro utility caddy that distributes weight properly.
💡
Queensland context: In summer heat, physical exertion raises injury risk significantly — your muscles fatigue faster, your reaction times slow, and you're more likely to cut corners on technique. Hydrate before and during work. If you feel lightheaded or exhausted — stop, cool down, contact Bonnie. Heat exhaustion is a WorkCover incident.

Hand and skin health — the most common occupational hazard in cleaning

Occupational dermatitis affects approximately 30% of cleaning workers over their careers. It's caused by repeated wet work and chemical exposure — and it starts slowly, then escalates. The people who take this seriously early have long, healthy careers. The ones who ignore it end up with skin conditions that limit what they can do.

What to do — every day

Gloves for ALL wet work — bathrooms, kitchens, mopping, applying any product. No exceptions. Refer to Module 4 on why this matters chemically.
Moisturise after every job — a thick, fragrance-free hand cream applied after washing your hands and removing gloves. This repairs the skin barrier that repeated wet work degrades.
Watch for early signs — dryness, redness, cracking, itchiness between fingers. These are early warnings. Report to Bonnie. Early treatment prevents it becoming a permanent condition.
Don't push through skin pain — cracked, bleeding skin with chemical exposure is an infection risk and a WorkCover issue. Address it.
Latex allergy — if you notice itching, rash, or hives after wearing latex gloves, switch to nitrile immediately and tell Bonnie. Latex allergy can escalate to serious anaphylaxis with repeated exposure.

Career development and your future at WoodBClean

What growth actually looks like here. Clear pathways from new starter to specialist to team leader — and how WoodBClean invests in people who commit to this team.

This is not just a job — unless you want it to be

Some people join WoodBClean for a job while they figure out what is next. Some join and build a genuine career here. Both are completely valid — and WoodBClean supports both.

What Bonnie wants you to know: the people who invest in their skills, show up consistently, and commit to the WoodBClean standard open real doors.
