Set your 90-day goal

The most effective way to grow is to decide what you are working toward. A 90-day goal gives you a concrete, achievable target that is close enough to feel real and far enough to require consistent effort.

Think about what you want to achieve in your first 90 days at WoodBClean and write it down. Then tell Bonnie. When someone else knows your goal, you are significantly more likely to achieve it.
Examples of strong 90-day goals
Complete all 14 modules and earn my full certification. · Become competent in bond cleans with zero callbacks. · Complete my first 3 government contract cleans independently. · Start my Airbnb specialisation and get my first 5-star property review.
Tell Bonnie your goal
Send Bonnie a message with your 90-day goal. She will check in with you, support you toward it, and celebrate it with you when you get there.
Review and reset every 90 days
Once you hit your goal — set a new one. Growth does not stop at 90 days. The best team members are always working toward something.
WoodBClean grows when its team members grow. Your goals and WoodBClean goals are the same thing. We are genuinely invested in your success.

Australian certifications — what's available and what it's worth

Qualifications in the cleaning industry open real doors — commercial contracts, specialist work, and significantly higher pay rates. These are real Australian certifications, not theoretical ones.

Certifications relevant to WoodBClean work

1
Certificate III in Cleaning Operations (CPC30319)
The industry-standard qualification for professional cleaners. Covers cleaning principles, safety, chemical handling, and specialised cleaning techniques. Opens doors to commercial contracts, government facilities, and institutional work. Approximate cost: $800–$2,000. Duration: 6–12 months part-time. Ask Bonnie about traineeship options that allow you to earn while you study.
2
IICRC Applied Microbial Remediation (Mould)
The international standard for mould remediation — this is the Level 2 pathway at WoodBClean. Certified technicians can handle large-scale mould remediation, insurance-backed jobs, and structural moisture work. Approximate cost: $1,500–$2,500. This is a specialist certification that commands significantly higher rates. Talk to Bonnie if this interests you.
3
IICRC Water Damage Restoration (WRT)
Covers water damage assessment, drying, and restoration. Relevant for flood and leak remediation work — a growing specialisation in Queensland. Opens insurance restoration contracts. Approximate cost: $1,200–$1,800.
4
White Card (Construction Induction)
Required to work on any construction site in Australia — including new build cleans. If you want to work on new builds regularly, you need a White Card. Cost: approximately $50–$120. One day course. Available through RTO providers throughout Queensland.
Bonnie is genuinely interested in supporting team members who want to upskill. If a certification aligns with WoodBClean's service offering — there may be support available. Have the conversation. Don't assume the answer is no.

Specialist Reference · Optional

Furniture and soft furnishings

An optional reference for subcontractors who want to expand their knowledge of furniture care. Not part of the core certification — use it when you need it.

Leather furniture care

Leather is one of the most common premium furniture materials — and one of the easiest to damage with the wrong product. Leather is a natural material that needs to be cleaned gently and conditioned to stay supple.
Do: Use a dedicated leather cleaner or a very lightly damp microfibre cloth for surface dust and light marks. Wipe in the direction of the grain.
Do: Use a leather conditioner occasionally to prevent cracking and drying — especially in air-conditioned environments.
Do: Blot liquid spills immediately with a clean dry cloth. Do not rub.
Never: Use all-purpose cleaners, bleach, vinegar, alcohol-based products, or any product not specifically designed for leather. Causes permanent drying, cracking, and discolouration.
Never: Saturate leather with moisture. Excess water causes leather to warp, crack, and mould.
Never: Use dark-coloured cloths on light leather. Dye transfer from cloths can stain lighter leather permanently.

Fabric upholstery care

Fabric upholstery varies enormously — from robust microsuede to delicate linen. Before applying any product, check the care label on the furniture if accessible. Look for W (water-based), S (solvent-based), W/S (either), or X (vacuum only).
Do: Vacuum fabric thoroughly with the upholstery attachment before any wet cleaning to remove loose debris and pet hair.
Do: Spot test any product in a hidden area and wait 5 minutes before proceeding.
Do: Blot stains — never rub. Rubbing pushes stains deeper and spreads them.
Never: Machine wash cushion covers without checking the care label. Many shrink or bleed colour.
Never: Over-wet fabric upholstery. Moisture trapped inside cushions causes mould and a persistent musty smell.

Timber furniture care

Timber furniture — tables, chairs, shelving, cabinetry — requires a gentle approach. The finish (lacquer, oil, wax, raw) determines what is safe to use.
Do: Dust first with a dry microfibre cloth, always following the wood grain direction.
Do: For sealed/lacquered timber, a lightly damp cloth with a small amount of pH-neutral cleaner is safe. Dry immediately.
Do: Use a furniture polish or oil appropriate for the finish type for oiled or waxed timber.
Never: Use excess water on timber furniture. Water causes swelling, white water marks, and warping.
Never: Use silicon-based polishes on natural timber — builds up over time and prevents the timber from breathing.

Before reading: why do you think professional cleaners use different coloured cloths for different areas of a property? What problem does this solve?

Cross-contamination. Using the same cloth in a bathroom and then on a kitchen bench transfers bacteria — including E. coli and salmonella — from one surface to another. The colour system creates an automatic, visible reminder that prevents this. Red for toilets and sanitary areas. Blue for general surfaces. Yellow for kitchens. Green for food areas or external. Always use the WoodBClean standard.

Stainless steel appliances and surfaces

Stainless steel appliances — fridges, dishwashers, rangehoods, ovens — are common in modern kitchens and require specific care to avoid scratching and streaking.
Do: Always wipe in the direction of the grain (the faint brushed lines). Cross-grain wiping causes micro-scratches that build up over time.
Do: Use a microfibre cloth with a small amount of glass cleaner or dedicated stainless steel cleaner for a streak-free finish.
Do: A tiny drop of baby oil or mineral oil on a dry cloth, buffed in the grain direction, gives a premium showroom finish and repels fingerprints.
Never: Use steel wool, abrasive scrubbers, or abrasive powders on stainless steel. Scratches the surface permanently.
Never: Use bleach on stainless steel. Causes pitting and discolouration over time.
